#6237. United Airlines Launches 11 New International Routes This Winter: See Full List Now

United Airlines is the second-largest international operator from the US, behind American Airlines. Of course, United's strength is long-haul, for which it is comfortably number one. In fact, the Star Alliance member is the world's second-largest long-haul carrier, after Emirates.

On Sunday, October 25, United (like other Northern Hemisphere airlines) switched to winter schedules based on IATA slot seasons. This will be maintained until Saturday, March 27, 2027. In this period, Cirium Diio data shows that United will have an average of 350 daily international departures, up by 2% compared to last winter. 11 additional routes help.

Schedule analysis shows that United will introduce, or resume, the following routes beyond the US border during the cold season. They are from five hubs. As they have all been announced, this article simply summarizes them and provides some context and information.

The October 31 launch of United's first service from Newark to St. Croix is not included. That is because the Caribbean destination is in the US Virgin Islands and is, therefore, considered domestic. United's three flights from Las Vegas to Tokyo Narita in January 2027 for the Consumer Electronics Show are also not featured.

Washington Dulles to Los Cabos (above photo is of the relaunch)

Houston Intercontinental to Tuxtla Gutiérrez (the following photo is from the relaunch)

Daily 737 MAX 9 (only until January 4, 2027)

Houston Intercontinental to Santo Domingo

3 weekly 737 MAX 8 (only until January 3, 2027)

No, it's a brand-new market for United; it'll coexist with Japan Airlines

* October 25, 2026, to March 27, 2027, only

When all airlines and US airports are considered, Cirium shows that United is the second-largest operator from the US to Mexico, behind American. United serves the transborder country from eight hubs and other airports. On a typical day, it has 86 daily departures to Mexico. For very obvious reasons, most of them — 46 daily and 53% of the total — are from Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

After a 13-year absence, flights from IAH to Tuxtla Gutiérrez have resumed. As such, United now serves 25 destinations in Mexico from the Texas hub. They include Tulum, to which various US airlines have stopped flying. United will join them, as it is pulling out in January 2027. Service to Chihuahua returns at the start of the summer 2027 season.

16 of the 25 airports see the regional jets of United Express. Ten markets are exclusively in the hands of such equipment, whether on the E175 operated by Mesa or SkyWest, the CRJ550 with GoJet, or the ERJ145 with CommutAir. The 50-seat CRJ550 is on one route: Monterrey (from February 11, 2027). The ERJ145 also has only one market: Puebla, 669 nautical miles (1,237 km) away. Six routes see both RJs and non-RJ narrowbodies, while nine do not see RJs at all.

Only one of the transcontinental services have seen United before. Find out more here!

Starting on December 11, flights from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to Sapporo will, of course, be a proper winter service. That's because the Japanese city is famous for being the gateway to skiing and other sporting activities and broader winter fun.

The other two upcoming long-haul routes — Los Angeles to Osaka and SFO to Okinawa — almost did not make the list. That's because the first departure from California will be on March 27, which is the final day of the northern aviation winter based on IATA slot seasons. The first service from Asia will be on March 28, the first day of the northern summer season. Okinawa will be a seasonal route, while Osaka will be flown year-round.

#6236. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

#6234. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

#6232. It's Official: Lufthansa Signs $1.2 Billion Deal To Purchase 44.9% Of TAP Air Portugal

Lufthansa Group and the Portuguese government have officially signed an agreement for the German aviation giant to acquire a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal for €1.025 billion (approximately $1.2 billion). The signing took place in Lisbon earlier today, nearly three weeks after Portugal selected Lufthansa ahead of rival Air France-KLM. The transaction remains subject to regulatory approval.

The agreement represents another milestone in Lufthansa's European airline consolidation strategy. It could add Lisbon as the group's seventh hub while significantly strengthening its position in Latin America. However, the deal also raises two important questions: how did Lufthansa beat Air France-KLM, the airline group that many experts favored, and can it replicate IAG's success with Iberia?

The agreement was officially signed at Lisbon Airport (LIS), with Lufthansa funding the acquisition entirely from existing liquidity. Euronews reports that the group could increase its holding to 49.9% by purchasing shares initially reserved for TAP employees, potentially lifting total consideration to €1.2 billion. Portugal will initially retain majority ownership, while European Commission approval is still required before completion.

Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr emphasized that the airlines' networks are complementary, particularly in South America and Brazil. Lisbon will become Lufthansa Group's seventh hub, with further growth planned across Portuguese-speaking Africa and North America. The group also expects up to €450 million in synergies, with most potentially achievable before acquiring majority ownership.

“Together with TAP's employees, we want to continue the airline's success story, preserve its Portuguese identity, and develop Lisbon into a Lufthansa Group hub.”

Lufthansa has also welcomed the possibility of TAP's full privatization, while its commitments include maintaining the airline's Portuguese identity, strengthening regional connectivity, and expanding investment in Portugal. The government has outlined potential fleet growth to 130 aircraft, while Lufthansa Technik's new facility near Porto should help increase the group's Portuguese workforce to more than 1,000 by 2030.

Air France-KLM initially appeared to be the more attractive buyer. While Lufthansa enjoys an existing relationship with TAP through Star Alliance, potentially simplifying commercial cooperation, the Franco-Dutch group seemed the more complementary partner with its hubs at Paris and Amsterdam. Most crucially, Air France-KLM wasn't already entangled with the integration of a prior acquisition, as Lufthansa is with ITA Airways.

But ultimately, the financial offer proved decisive. Portugal revealed that Lufthansa's proposal was up to 16% higher than Air France-KLM's, with less uncertainty. Both bidders had improved their proposals during final negotiations, and their strategic commitments had become broadly comparable. Prime Minister Luís Montenegro described Lufthansa as "the choice that best protected Portugal's national interests."

Lufthansa's experience integrating SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, and ITA Airways provides another potential advantage. Its multi-brand model allows carriers to retain their identities while sharing commercial and operational resources. However, TAP's minority ownership structure presents challenges: Lufthansa must deliver substantial synergies without initially enjoying the control associated with its other acquisitions.

The $1.2 billion investment is more than three times what it paid for 41% of ITA back in 2025. So why is it splurging on a smaller European carrier? Brazil provides the answer. The group estimates its share of Europe–Latin America traffic at approximately 9%, rising to a calculated 20% when TAP is included. More specifically, Lisbon's established connections to Brazil offer access to markets where Lufthansa's existing network is comparatively limited, helping it compete more effectively with IAG and Air France-KLM.

The obvious comparison is the creation of IAG and the transformation of Iberia following its 2011 merger with British Airways. After restructuring, Iberia developed into one of Europe's most profitable airlines, recording a 16.2% operating margin and €1.31 billion in operating profit in 2025. Its Europe–Latin America and Caribbean capacity reached a record 5.5 million seats, demonstrating the financial potential of a strong transatlantic network.

Lufthansa hopes to replicate that success through coordinated schedules, purchasing, distribution, and stronger connecting traffic. However, Iberia's turnaround occurred under IAG's full ownership, whereas Lufthansa must initially work alongside the Portuguese government. With TAP also facing profitability pressures, the €1 billion investment is a significant bet that its valuable Brazilian network can deliver an Iberia-style transformation.

World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and I've loved redeeming my World of Hyatt points over the years on everything from cheap and cheerful Category 1 airport hotels to luxurious bespoke properties on idyllic Greek islands.

I knew that the program had expanded the ways to redeem points beyond hotel stays to experiences via its Find experiences platform. But I've never given it much thought, assuming the value (or the experiences themselves) wouldn't be that great.

So, when Hyatt recently invited me to an event that it sponsors, the Laver Cup tournament at London's The O2 arena, I jumped at the chance to go as a tennis enthusiast. I'd been to The O2 countless times for concerts and thought I knew the venue pretty well. But Hyatt was auctioning off a luxury experience in the ultra-VIP Legends Club, a space I didn't even know existed that turned out to be on a completely different level of luxury, in part due to its courtside seats for watching the action.

Seeing how few Hyatt points the winning bids went for, especially given this impressive level of premium hospitality and access, I came to the realization that this might just be the most valuable way to redeem World of Hyatt points.

Related: This is how you do a luxury all-inclusive: Zoetry Mallorca, bookable with Hyatt points

Find is World of Hyatt's experiences platform, where members can book everything from fitness workshops and chef's table dinners to Broadway tickets, paying with either cash or World of Hyatt points. You don't need to stay at a Hyatt hotel to take part, though some experiences include accommodations.

Most Find experiences are advertised with a fixed price — and that's where you might struggle to get outsize value. When TPG travel writer Rachel Craft tested a fixed-price Find dining package in Denver, it delivered less value than TPG's valuation of World of Hyatt points at the time, and she concluded that members would probably get more value redeeming their points for hotel stays.

Auctions work differently. A small number of limited-time experiences, often tied to Hyatt's sports sponsorships, go to the highest bidder, with members bidding in points rather than paying a set price.

Before you bid, it's worth knowing the rules:

Auctions are usually only a small portion of the Find options available at any one time, so here's how you can find them:

The Laver Cup packages were a savvy example of just how much value a Find auction can deliver.

Each of the three packages Hyatt auctioned included:

Starting with priority, fast-track entry to the venue, the Legends Club was a significant step up in luxury from anything else I've seen at The O2. It even surpassed my impression of the Virgin Red Room, a corporate suite at The O2 that can be booked with Virgin Red points.

The two-level hospitality suite (usually hidden behind the stage at traditional concerts) was huge and opened onto the arena, with a perfect view down the baseline.

Before the play started, there was even a Q&A with tennis legend Andy Murray, which isn't something you get with a regular ticket.

Premium food and drinks were included from 90 minutes before the session until the final ball, and the Champagne kept flowing the entire time.

When it was time for the tennis, I headed down to my own courtside seat in the second row. I was so close to the current No. 3 player in the world, Carlos Alcaraz, that I could almost have reached out and touched him.

I didn't stay at the Park Hyatt this time, but having toured the hotel, I can see why it would make the package even more appealing, with spacious rooms, marble bathrooms, views over the Thames and a 65-foot indoor pool.

Published all-in prices for a single Legends Club ticket ranged from $1,329 to $2,652 for Friday night and from $1,461 to $2,916 for either Saturday session, depending on the seat.

Standard rooms started at $633 per night when TPG reviewed the Park Hyatt, and the hotel's 60-minute "Back to Brilliance" massage cost $279 per person. Add the two-night stay and hotel credit, and I estimate each package was worth between $5,000 and $8,000 before assigning any value to the transfers.

A search engine index of Hyatt’s official Find homepage shows Hyatt auctioned off three Laver Cup packages with Legends Club single-session tickets and Park Hyatt accommodations (plus the above-mentioned inclusions) with winning bids of 81,583, 120,560 and 160,000 points, although the closed listings are no longer visible on the live page.

TPG's October 2026 valuations assign a value of 1.65 cents to every World of Hyatt point. By that valuation, the winning bids were worth about $1,346, $1,989 and $2,640, respectively. Even using the low end of my estimated package value, those redemptions delivered about 6.1, 4.1 and 3.1 cents per point, respectively, or roughly 1.9 to 3.7 times TPG's valuation, a spectacular result.

Put another way, the Category 8 Park Hyatt London River Thames costs 35,000 to 75,000 World of Hyatt points per night for a standard room, so two nights can cost 70,000 to 150,000 points. The two lower bids were below the 150,000-point threshold required for two standard award nights on top-priced dates, while the highest bid was only 10,000 points higher.

Of course, not every auction will deliver this much value. Popular experiences, such as Formula One races, can attract plenty of competition, and you have no control over where the bidding ends. However, you can decide up front what an experience is worth to you and stop bidding if the price goes past that amount.

World of Hyatt members earn points on eligible Hyatt stays and Find bookings paid for with cash, but a credit card can be the quickest way to build your balance for an auction.

You can choose between two cobranded cards:

Or, you can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt from the following cards:

Chase Ultimate Rewards points held in Chase Sapphire Reserve and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business accounts transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio.

Points held in Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred accounts transfer at a 4:3 ratio, meaning 1,000 Ultimate Rewards points become 750 World of Hyatt points.

Bilt Points currently transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio through Dec. 31, 2026. The ratio will drop to 4:3 on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: How many Hyatt points do you need to transfer before the Sapphire Reserve beats the Sapphire Preferred?

Fixed-price Find experiences still would not usually tempt me away from a hotel redemption, but auctions are a different story.

This was easily the most luxurious sporting experience I have ever attended, from the VIP entry to the spectacular views and the hospitality of the Legends Club, which offered everything I could imagine, including proximity to some of the world's best tennis players.

Factor in the accommodations, transfers, food-and-beverage credits and other perks, and it's clear this is an exceptional way to redeem World of Hyatt points. You'll potentially considerably exceed our valuation of these excellent hotel points by redeeming them this way.

The 2027 Laver Cup will be played at the Intuit Dome near Los Angeles from Sept. 24 to 26, 2027. As the official hotel partner, look out for Hyatt Find experiences and auctions for next year's tournament.

Want to take advantage of Rosewood Elite benefits, including a space available room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. His team may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

Luxury hotel group Rosewood has just kicked off its best sale of the year, offering savings of up to 30%, and it’s exclusively available through Rosewood Elite travel advisors. If you’ve been considering a stay at a Rosewood, this would be a great time to book.

With the Rosewood Beyond promotion, guests can save 30% off the best available rate when booking a Rosewood property through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. To cover the basics:

#6227. New Cathay Pacific “Halo Suites” First Class For Boeing 777-9s

In late 2024, Cathay Pacific unveiled its new Aria Suites business class, which is progressively being introduced on the carrier’s Boeing 777-300ER fleet. While we know Cathay Pacific is introducing a new first class product, it’ll take some time before we see that in service.

In light of everything going on — the introduction of Cathay Pacific’s new business class, the delays to the Boeing 777X, the products being introduced by competitors, etc. — I’d like to cover the latest when it comes to Cathay Pacific’s new first class.

We’ve known for years that Cathay Pacific plans to introduce new first and business class products on its Boeing 777-9s. The airline has 35 of these aircraft on order, and they’re expected to become the carrier’s flagship aircraft.

Note that not all Cathay Pacific 777-9s are expected to get first class. The expectation is that somewhere around 20 of them will feature the cabin, while the remaining will feature business class, premium economy, and economy.

Initially the aircraft was supposed to enter service as of 2020, though due to delays stemming from a variety of reasons, the plane is now slated to be delivered in 2027 at the earliest.

Many airlines were planning on introducing new “flagship” products on their 777-9s, though the seven year delay has obviously not been ideal for that, and has caused many airlines to fall behind with their premium products. I would imagine that Cathay Pacific was planning on debuting its new business class on 777-9s, but now decided to install it on 777-300ERs.

While Cathay Pacific has moved forward with introducing its new business class, the airline only plans to introduce a new first class as of 2027, on Boeing 777-9s. Understandably, one major concern here is when 777-9s will actually enter service for Cathay Pacific.

At this point, the aircraft will enter commercial service in the second half of 2027 at the absolute earliest, and Cathay Pacific isn’t even the launch customer. So it could very well be 2028 before we see the first Cathay Pacific 777-9.

In 2023, Cathay Pacific applied for a trademark for “The Aria Suites,” which is the carrier’s new business class. The airline also applied for a trademark for “The Halo Suites,” and this is specifically intended to cover “luxury and first class air transportation services.”

For what it’s worth, the two patents were filed just a few weeks apart. While we can’t say anything with certainty, I’d be willing to bet with that this will in fact be the name of Cathay Pacific’s new first class product.

We know that Cathay Pacific has been working on developing its new first class product for many years (it was supposed to be ready in 2020, based on the initial Boeing 777-9 delivery timeline). We also know that Cathay Pacific is planning something truly spectacular. However, there hasn’t been any official indication as to what we can expect (though rumor has it that we could get a “tease” in the coming months).

Back in 2019, Cathay Pacific applied for a patent for a new first class product, and… wow! Let me emphasize that I can’t guarantee this will be Cathay Pacific’s new first class, though I think it’s very possible. I’d highly recommend reading the whole application, as it actually contains a couple of different concepts.

Below is the diagram that’s displayed, and if I’m understanding this correctly, the plan is that figures five through eight reflect what Cathay Pacific is hoping to offer.

This appears to be based on Paperclip Design’s Peacock Suites concept. The below pictures should give you a sense of just how spectacular this product might be (though I’d expect Cathay Pacific to have a customized version of this, so don’t expect it to be exactly like this).

This product looks absolutely wild, and I’m in disbelief that we could see anything like this introduced. It almost looks more like The Etihad Residence than a standard first class product. Heck, it almost looks more like what you’d expect on a private jet.

A couple of years back, former Cathay Pacific Chairman Patrick Healy has called the new product “mindblowing,” and “a really, really special product and very impressive.”

This would likely blow away the best first class products in the world, like Air France’s 777 first class, Emirates’ 777 first class, and Japan Airlines’ A350 first class. In terms of other first class products on the horizon, we know that Singapore Airlines will be unveiling a new first class shortly, and Qatar Airways is working on a new first class, but it’s not a sure bet yet.

Due to ongoing delivery delays with the Boeing 777-9, the carrier’s plan to transition its fleet is proving to be anything but straightforward.

Cathay Pacific is currently retrofitting its 777-300ER fleet with the new Aria Suites business class. As the airline retrofits its 777-300ERs, it’s also removing first class from those planes (assuming they have them). We’re seeing a combination of three-cabin aircraft reconfigured (with business class, premium economy, and economy), along with some four-cabin aircraft (with first class).

At this point, Cathay Pacific has just six planes remaining with first class. In the past, the airline has acknowledged that it may hold off on reconfiguring some jets, so that it can maintain even a small fleet with first class seats, for markets where it’s really needed. However, with the extent of the delays, one wonders if Cathay Pacific really wants to put the fleet retrofit project on hold, just to preserve a few dozen first class seats.

Cathay Pacific’s first class is an excellent, spacious product. While this isn’t the world’s most private first class, it is one of my favorites. On top of that, the soft product is very good.

Cathay Pacific plans to introduce a new first class product, though only on the 777-9, and not on the 777-300ER. You can expect this product to be introduced as of late 2027 at the earliest, assuming the Boeing 777X actually gets certified (that’s a big “if”).

Based on some filings, it would appear that Cathay Pacific will name its new first class “The Halo Suites,” and some diagrams suggest that this will be an unbelievably good product. I can’t wait to learn more. Rumor has it that we could get our first official tease of this product in the coming months, though who knows, that may be delayed yet again.

What do you make of what we know about Cathay Pacific’s new first class?

#6226. Delta Plans Another Austin Route

Delta is expanding its Austin, Texas, network with a new daily route set to launch next spring.

The carrier will begin flights between Austin and Northwest Arkansas National Airport, which serves Fayetteville and the surrounding region, on March 7, 2027. SkyWest will operate the route under the Delta Connection brand using an Embraer E175.

Service from Northwest Arkansas to Austin begins March 8. Tickets are now on sale.

Flights will depart Austin at 8:59 p.m. and arrive in Northwest Arkansas at 10:49 p.m. The return flight will leave at 6 a.m. and arrive in Austin at 7:50 a.m. All times are local.

“Connecting Central Texas and Northwest Arkansas with new nonstop service brings two dynamic, growing regions closer together while giving our customers even more choice and convenience,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement.

Guitart described the addition as another example of the airline’s investment in Austin.

Delta has been building its Austin operation, with plans to offer more than 70 peak-day departures to approximately 30 destinations by summer 2027. That expansion includes new service to Paris and San Diego, a second daily flight to San Jose, California, and year-round service to Cancun, Mexico.

#6225. The One 737 Variant That Saved Boeing's Narrowbody Line

Today, the aircraft is known for being the second-best-selling commercial jetliner of all time, behind only the competing Airbus A320. In the late 1970s, however, the Boeing 737 was not the dominant narrowbody that everyone knows it to be today. That was the Boeing 727, a larger, three-engined aircraft used for medium-length flights around the world, similar in size to modern 737 variants. Back then, the 737 was Boeing's small narrowbody, essentially used like a large regional jet, while the 727 dominated the industry.

In the late 1970s, however, the 727's three-engined layout was increasingly becoming obsolete, as the plane burned too much fuel for its size and range. Boeing would respond by developing an all-new, twin-engined layout that essentially did everything the 727 did but better. At the same time, there was demand for an improved 737 after the success of the 737-200. As such, Boeing began studies on a new 737 variant in 1979, and in 1984, the company released the massively successful 737-300.

By 1979, the 737 line was essentially the 737-200 Advanced. Slightly stretched from the original 737-100, the 737-200 became a popular choice worldwide for regional routes, competing against the McDonnell Douglas DC-9. The Advanced became the production standard in 1971, incorporating aerodynamic and technical improvements to improve payload and range. It was a massive success, but the 737 was also aging by the late 1970s, creating demand for an improved version.

The most noticeable difference with the 737-300 was its extended fuselage, increasing passenger capacity and lowering unit costs. The aircraft's wing was tweaked for better aerodynamics. Boeing swapped out the 1960s-era Pratt & Whitney JT8Ds for the new CFM56-3 high-bypass turbofan, and the plane received a new vertical stabilizer design, while the cabin and flight deck were modernized. As a whole, the 737-300 was a significantly more capable, more efficient, and more advanced version of the already popular 737.

The 737-300 proved to be a very successful aircraft, with Boeing receiving hundreds of orders for the type after its entry into service in 1984. At this point, the aircraft was competing mainly against the McDonnell Douglas MD-80, but it was more fuel-efficient while carrying slightly fewer passengers, and it was used by many airlines to replace older 727s as well. In the 1980s, the market also lined up well for the 737-300 to become a core part of Boeing's narrowbody offering alongside the 757.

By the late 1970s, both of Boeing's two narrowbody products were popular, but aging. The 737 was revitalized as the 737-300, while the airframer decided on a clean-sheet twinjet to succeed the 727. The 757 carried more passengers and payload than the 727, while having superior takeoff performance, a longer range, and better fuel burn. It was an appealing aircraft for airlines wanting an aircraft larger than the 737, and it also proved effective in replacing 707s and DC-8s on transcontinental flights in the US, given its range.

However, the 757 wasn't as desirable as Boeing may have hoped when it debuted in 1983. The US market began shifting towards smaller aircraft, and the 757 seated more passengers than the 727. Fuel prices also dropped, and the 757 was an expensive aircraft to buy.

Many airlines chose to simply keep their depreciated 727s longer, while others bought the cheaper MD-80, which also entered service earlier than the 757. The 737-300 became a crucial aircraft, as it occupied this space of being more fuel-efficient than prior jetliners, while also being smaller and cheaper to buy than the 757. It became a popular replacement for the 727 as a result.

Orders for the 757 picked up in the late 1980s, and the aircraft went on to be a successful program. However, it was during this time with the 737-300 that the aircraft started transitioning towards becoming the core of Boeing's narrowbody lineup, whereas it was the 727 that dominated sales in the past. This shift only became more apparent as Boeing was able to further iterate on the design by releasing an even larger variant as well as a smaller version that could directly succeed the 737-200.

This aviation marvel that combines power, efficiency, and record-breaking seating in one sleek package.

While the 737-300 was stretched by about three seat rows over the 737-200, the 757 could seat an additional 60 or 70 passengers compared to the 737-300. This left a major hole in Boeing's narrowbody lineup, especially as the MD-80 was larger than the 737-300. With strong demand from airlines for a larger 737, Boeing stretched the airframe by about three to four rows, creating the 737-400. Debuting in 1988 with Piedmont Airlines, the 737-400 also proved to be an attractive aircraft like its older sibling.

What makes a stretch aircraft like the 737-400 attractive is its low per-seat costs, since the plane burns almost the same fuel as the 737-300 while offering significantly more seats. However, not all airlines need an aircraft that can seat as many as 188 passengers, and even the 737-300 was larger than the first-generation 737. As such, Boeing shrank the fuselage to create the 737-500, which entered service in 1990 to directly succeed the 737-200. Not only was the aircraft smaller, but it had the best range and takeoff performance of any 737 variant.

On its own, the 737-300's sales might not look all that impressive, as Boeing sold 1,113 examples. However, the 737-300 transformed the 737 into a family, with the 737-400 and 737-500 variants each offering something different to appeal to a wider range of customers. The 737-400 received 486 orders, while the 737-500 received 389 orders, bringing the 737 Classic up to 1,988 sales in total. In contrast, the 757 (including the later 757-300) received 1,049 orders, while the competing MD-80 received 1,191 orders.

European newcomer Airbus had made a name for itself in the 1970s with its A300, a medium-sized twinjet widebody that outsold both of its rivals (the McDonnell Douglas DC-10 and Lockheed L-1011 TriStar). It also later developed the A310 as a smaller derivative with better range, to more limited success. After years of design studies, it officially launched the clean-sheet single-aisle A320 in 1984. But to truly be successful, Airbus couldn't just build a plane as good as what the Americans had made; it needed to make a better one.

The A320-100 entered service in 1988 with Air France, with the improved A320-200 following shortly afterwards (this became the production standard). The aircraft was larger than the 737-400, which entered service the same year, and it could fly farther than any 737 variant while also cruising faster. In addition, the A320 was a significant step forward in terms of technology, introducing innovations such as a full glass cockpit, digital fly-by-wire control systems, and sidestick controls.

The 737 Classic was an appealing aircraft to 737 operators and those loyal to American manufacturers, but Airbus was ruthless with its A320. It notably sold the aircraft to Northwest Airlines, followed by United Airlines, which was widely expected to order the 737-400 at the time. The loss of the United order in particular prompted Boeing to revisit the 737 to better match the A320. What followed next was the most competitive 737 generation that Boeing had turned out yet.

The aircraft will be replaced by other highly capable, but smaller, widebodies.

The 737NG was the most significant overhaul to the 737 line yet. Boeing slightly stretched the aircraft to create the 737-700, while also upgrading the engines to the CFM56-7. In addition, the wing was fully redesigned for the 737NG, while the interior and flight deck were significantly modernized. The 737-700, positioned as a successor to the 737-300, proved to be a valiant competitor against the similarly sized Airbus A319-100. However, it was the 737-800, which succeeded the 737-400, that became the superstar of the family.

The 737-800 would compete directly against the A320-200, and it actually held some advantages. The aircraft was lighter than the A320-200, yet it could carry more passengers, and the 737-800 also had transcontinental range. The 737-800 ended up slightly outselling the A320-200, despite debuting about a decade later. Boeing would also stretch the aircraft to create the 737-900 and the later 737-900ER, but both of these proved ineffective at competing against the A321-200.

Boeing reengined and lightly improved the 737-800 and 737-900ER to create the 737 MAX 8 and 737 MAX 9, while the other MAX variants have more differences from prior models. However, these variants are very similar to their predecessors. The 737NG, however, was a much more thorough improvement compared to its predecessor, necessitated by the arrival of a competitor that was designed to render the 737 Classic obsolete.

#6222. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6221. Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card Amex Offers Deal: Save $200 On $900+ Flight

The Amex Offers program frequently offers promotions that can save you money on flights, hotel stays, etc. There’s a new Amex Offers deal that seems to be specific to one co-branded Marriott card, and it’s incredibly lucrative.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) seems to have a new targeted Amex Offers deal whereby you can earn $200 back when you spend $900+ on airfare.

This is really straightforward — targeted members just need to register for the Amex Offers deal, and then spend $900+ across one or more transactions by February 28, 2027.

You can reach that spending threshold through one or more qualifying purchases, and the flights need to be booked directly with airlines (so not through a third party). There are no restrictions as to which airline you can book through, so you can use this both for US and foreign carriers, which is awesome.

Officially Amex Offers deals are all targeted, though this one at least seems to be pretty widely targeted. It seems that it’s specific to this card, and that most people with the card are eligible for the offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card has a steep annual fee. Personally, it’s a card that I have, and one that I find to represent a good value, thanks to the variety of perks it offers. However, an easy $200 in savings beyond the expected value sure helps even more with making the math work!

The card ordinarily earns 3x Bonvoy points per dollar spent on airfare, and I value those points at 0.7 cents each, for a 2.1% return. So if you spent exactly $900 on a ticket, you’d get a $200 statement credit plus 2,700 Bonvoy points, which I value at an extra $19 return, for a total return of around 24%. That’s excellent.

Even if you don’t have an immediate ticket you want to book, most major US airlines let you bank credit if you buy a ticket and then decide that you no longer want to travel. So you could typically buy a $900 (non-basic) ticket, and essentially pick up that much credit with an airline for around $700. That’s a great value, assuming you can use the credit before it expires.

Amex Offers has a new deal that can save you $200+ on the cost of an airfare purchase of $900+. This seems to be specific to the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, and it’s widely targeted. This is an easy opportunity to save well over 20% on the cost of an airline ticket with few strings attached, so it’s worth taking advantage of, if eligible.

Are you eligible for this Amex Offers deal, and do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6220. Condor Plans To Open First-Ever Lounge At Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3

Germany’s second largest airline, Condor, plans to open its own lounge for the first time ever. However, some more patience will be required, and details are also still quite limited.

Earlier this year, we saw Frankfurt Airport (FRA) open its new Terminal 3, which is the airport’s first new terminal in decades. We’ve already seen all airlines that previously occupied Terminal 2 move to Terminal 3.

The long term plan is that Terminal 1 will be exclusively for Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, while Terminal 3 will be for all other airlines. Meanwhile Terminal 2 may eventually be rebuilt, as Lufthansa hopes to take it over as well, but that’s a very long term vision.

As of now, the only airline that hasn’t yet completed the move to Terminal 3 is Condor, which is Germany’s second largest airline. The carrier still operates out of Terminal 1, and uses Lufthansa lounges for its customers, despite Lufthansa’s disdain for the carrier.

The expectation is that Condor will make the move to Frankfurt Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027. As part of that, the airline also plans to open two lounges in the terminal, as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. The expectation is that one will be a Schengen lounge, while the other will be a non-Schengen lounge.

The catch is that the lounges will only open later in 2027, due to the pace of construction. While the company’s CEO confirmed these plans in a meeting with employees, publicly the airline has only confirmed that “we are currently in discussions with our partners at Terminal 3 of Frankfurt Airport to explore the possibilities for Condor’s own lounge offering.”

No details are yet known about what kind of amenities the lounges will offer… I’m definitely curious to see what they come up with, as it’s always interesting when an airline opens a lounge for the first time!

Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 is getting quite a nice selection of lounges. As things currently stand:

On top of that, we know that Qatar Airways is opening two lounges in the non-Schengen area of the terminal, which will be for passengers traveling on oneworld airlines.

Condor is expected to move to Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027, as it’s the last (and largest) airline to make the move to the terminal. We now officially know that Condor is planning on opening two lounges in the terminal, though they’ll likely only open in late 2027.

It’s exciting to see the airline open lounges for the first time, and only time will tell how this plays out…

What do you make of Condor opening lounges for the first time?

#6219. JetBlue Hikes Checked Bag Fees Again To $50, A 43% Increase In Just 2 Years

JetBlue has raised checked baggage fees for the second time this year, increasing the minimum charge for a first checked bag on most North American and Caribbean routes from $39 to $50 each way. The new prices apply to tickets purchased on or after November 3, 2026. Compared with the $35 minimum in effect in May 2024, the latest adjustment represents an increase of approximately 43%. Passengers who wait until the airport, travel during peak periods, or check additional luggage will pay considerably more.

The increase affects more than basic economy customers. Travelers holding standard Main and Main Flex fares are also subject to the higher charges unless they qualify for complimentary baggage through an eligible fare, loyalty programs, or JetBlue credit card. The airline says the changes will help offset rising fuel and operating expenses while allowing it to keep advertised base fares competitive. The move could also prompt another round of baggage-fee increases across the US airline industry.

For flights within the United States, Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean, JetBlue’s first checked bag now costs $50 each way during off-peak periods when purchased online or through the app more than 24 hours before departure. The price rises to $55 during peak travel periods. Customers who add a bag within 24 hours of departure pay $60 off-peak or $70 during peak dates.

Additional luggage has become more expensive, too, as reported by Thrifty Traveler. A second checked bag costs $70 off-peak and $75 during peak periods when prepaid, increasing to $75 and $85, respectively, when purchased closer to departure. A third checked bag carries a $200 charge regardless of the travel date. On transatlantic flights to Europe, the first bag on the cheapest economy fares starts at $80, with late purchases reaching $100.

Booking timing can significantly affect the final bill. A passenger checking one bag for a peak-season round trip could pay $110 by prepaying, or $140 if the bag is purchased at the airport. Tickets purchased before November 3 remain subject to the previous fee schedule, so the increase does not retroactively affect existing bookings.

The latest adjustment continues a series of increases that have made checked luggage substantially more expensive on JetBlue. In May 2024, the minimum fee for a first checked bag on domestic, Canadian, Caribbean, and Latin American routes was $35. It rose to $39 in March 2026 before reaching $50 in November. The change from $35 to $50 represents a 42.9% increase over roughly two and a half years.

JetBlue also varies baggage prices according to demand, booking timing, and route type rather than applying one universal charge. Peak periods include much of the summer, from late May through early September, as well as major holiday travel dates. March is the only month in 2027 without a designated peak travel date, according to the published schedule. This pricing structure allows the airline to collect more when demand is strongest.

Several customer groups remain exempt. JetBlue Mint passengers receive checked baggage as part of their fare, while TrueBlue Mosaic members receive one or two complimentary bags depending on their status level. Eligible JetBlue Plus, Business, and Premier credit cardholders can also receive a free first checked bag for themselves and up to three companions when the card is used to book the flight.

Delta Air Lines joins United and JetBlue in hiking checked baggage fees, following a sharp rise in global jet fuel prices.

JetBlue directly attributed the latest increase to rising fuel and operating costs. A spokesperson said the airline is adjusting baggage charges to help keep base fares competitive while giving customers the option to pay only for services they use. Higher fuel prices have placed additional pressure on airline operating costs. US carriers generally do not hedge fuel purchases to the same extent as some international competitors, leaving them more immediately exposed when market prices climb. Baggage fees offer one way to recover some of those expenses without increasing the headline fare displayed during flight searches.

JetBlue’s financial position adds another consideration. The airline reported a $257 million third-quarter loss, renewing questions about its ability to return to sustained profitability. It denied speculation about a possible bankruptcy last week. Ancillary charges can generate additional revenue without making the initial ticket price appear less competitive, particularly among customers comparing fares across multiple airlines.

JetBlue has previously been an early mover on baggage pricing. After its March 2026 increase, other major US carriers followed with their own adjustments within weeks. That history does not guarantee another industry-wide response, but it gives competitors an opportunity to raise fees without being first. For passengers, the latest change is another reminder that the advertised airfare represents only part of the cost of flying with checked luggage.

United Airlines will expand to northern Mexico next spring despite a cloudy outlook.

The Star Alliance carrier will return to Chihuahua Airport (CUU) in northern Mexico from Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) beginning March 28, 2027.

Edibray Gómez Gallegos, the secretary of tourism of Chihuahua state, said the new route will increase connectivity for the state and "reflects growing interest among North American travelers in discovering the many tourist attractions Chihuahua has to offer."

United last served the IAH-CUU route in 2020, according to schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. It will join American Airlines among U.S. carriers serving the airport.

A spacious Bombardier CRJ-550 will be used on the route. The plane, originally a 70-seat CRJ-700, is fitted with 10 first-class, 20 extra-legroom economy and 20 economy seats.

Other news: United is bringing its nicest plane (with the Polaris Studios) to a city that never sees it

The new CUU route comes as airlines around the globe have been forced to adjust to soaring fuel costs.

United CEO Scott Kirby has previously warned that United has “no hesitation to cut capacity of flights that are losing money” in 2027 if fuel prices stay elevated as expected.

For context, the average global price for a gallon of jet fuel stood at $4.56 during the week ending Oct. 30, up 3.8% from the previous month's average, according to data from trade group IATA.

For now, however, the carrier remains mostly in growth mode. This new route is the latest in a bevy of additions from United in 2027.

The airline will add at least five new routes from San Francisco International Airport (SFO), including to Charleston International Airport (CHS) in South Carolina and Richmond International Airport (RIC) in Virginia, and from O’Hare International Airport (ORD) in Chicago to L.F. Wade International Airport (BDA) in Bermuda.

And then there is United’s blockbuster 10-route summer long-haul expansion that will add destinations including Luxembourg Airport (LUX) and Ljubljana Airport (LJU) in Slovenia to its map.

It is not all growth for United next year, though. The airline will end service to Tulum International Airport (TQO) in Mexico in January.

Overall, these additions and cuts underscore United's efforts to grow its network while keeping an eye on profitability.

#6216. Southwest’s New Credit Card Bonuses Offer Up To 90,000 Points Toward Companion Pass—Last Chance Before Rules Change

Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Southwest’s Companion Pass lets someone fly with you for just taxes and fees, even when you redeem points for your own ticket. For someone who flies Southwest with a partner a few times a year, it’s the single best deal in domestic air travel. And the easiest way to earn it is about to disappear.

There’s still a final window to use an 80,000- or 90,000-point credit card initial bonus toward a pass valid through December 31, 2027. You need to apply by December 2, 2026 and get approved. Neither bonus gets you all the way there on its own, but both give you a huge head start.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee. This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation: First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group. You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller. First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares. The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar. I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference. How Close These Bonuses Get You To Companion Pass Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive. You still have to meet the initial bonus spending requirement within the first 3 months from account opening. The transition rule doesn’t extend that deadline. I’m a former Companion Pass holder, and a promotional Companion Pass holder.Southwest still represents about 40% of the seats out of my home airport in Austin. Even with all the changes they’ve made, being able to bring someone along on those flights for just the taxes is huge. Before applying, you can’t currently hold a Southwest personal credit card, and you can’t have received an initial bonus on any Southwest personal card in the past 24 months. Southwest business and employee cards are excluded from that restriction. Chase’s usual 5/24 rule also applies: generally, you need fewer than 5 new credit card accounts on your credit report in the past 24 months. If you’re eligible, can handle the required spending, and have a path to the remaining qualifying points, I’d take advantage of this before December 2. #6215. Park Hyatt Phu Quoc, Vietnam, Opening Soon, And I’m Intrigued!

Back in 2019, plans were announced for an exciting new Park Hyatt resort in Vietnam. The property has been massively behind schedule on its planned 2022 opening. Several months ago, the hotel started accepting reservations for stays as of March 2027. There’s now a positive update, as the timeline has been moved forward to December 2026, so it’s just weeks away.

The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 8, 2026. The delays on this property have been endless, so it’s nice to see the timeline moved forward for once. Here’s to hoping that there are no last minute delays.

For those not familiar with Phu Quoc, it’s Vietnam’s largest island, and half of the island is in a national park and UNESCO site. The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is expected to feature a total of 168 keys, including 114 rooms and suites, and 54 private pool villas. This is Park Hyatt’s first resort in Vietnam, and second property in the country, after the Park Hyatt Saigon.

The resort is located on the southwestern tip of Phu Quoc Island, and is developed on 160 acres of land, bordered by a mile-long white sand beach on one side, and lush hills on the other side. The Park Hyatt is a 30-minute drive from Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC).

Details about the property are fairly limited, though here are some things we do know:

Below are some renderings of the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc. Given that we’ve had the same renderings for years and the property has been delayed year after year, I can’t help but wonder if the actual property looks anything like the renderings.

With the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc bookable, what are rates like? If you’re looking to redeem World of Hyatt points, this is a Category 7 property, meaning that a free night redemption will cost anywhere from 25,000 to 55,000 points per night, assuming a standard room is available. I value World of Hyatt points at around 1.4 cents each, so that puts the “cost” of a redemption at $350-770 per night.

When it comes to cash rates, they seem to start at just over $700 per night, and that’s before the 13.4% in taxes and service charges, so we’re talking about entry level rates of over $800 per night all-in.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

Depending on the award pricing for the nights you’re looking at, redeeming points here could potentially be a very good value.

While I’ve visited major cities in Vietnam several times before, I’ve never gone there for a beach vacation, so I’m intrigued by this property, especially given the value of World of Hyatt points, plus of World of Hyatt Globalist status.

Based on what I’ve heard, currently the top properties on the island are the JW Marriott Phu Quoc, the InterContinental Phu Quoc, and the Regent Phu Quoc. Many people have told me that these properties are among the best of their respective portfolios.

I’m curious, though, for those who have been to Phu Quoc, is it worth a trek from the United States? I’m sure it’s gorgeous and I’ll certainly take Vietnamese food over Caribbean food, but is it otherwise worth traveling that far out of the way?

It’s funny how my preferences in that regard have changed over the years. 15 years ago, I’d almost exclusively take beach vacations in Southeast Asia, given the generally higher standard of everything (service, hotels, etc.), plus the more reasonable prices.

However, as I’ve gotten older, my opinion has changed. For one, the jet lag becomes more challenging the older I get, and can take away from relaxation. Furthermore, flight award options just aren’t as exciting as they were over a decade ago. Like, easily being able to always snag Cathay Pacific first class awards was a great reason to vacation in Asia, as far as I’m concerned. 😉 But that’s no longer so easy.

But I also have another motive here. I’m intrigued by airline startup Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is just taking delivery of some Airbus A330s. So if I can fly an ex-American A330 directly to here, I’d sure find that to be amusing! For that matter, I really love the Capella hotel brand, and I’ve heard the Capella Hanoi is among the best in the portfolio, so I’d really love to visit that, and pair it with a visit here.

A Park Hyatt property is expected to open in Phu Quoc, Vietnam, and it’s now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. This property has been under development for eons, and it’s over four years behind schedule on opening. With the opening being just weeks away, here’s to hoping that the timeline finally actually sticks.

Do you plan on checking out the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc?
