#6214. WestJet Vs. Porter Airlines: Which Carrier Is More Premium In 2026?

Canadian air travel has long been defined by a strict dual-class hierarchy, with flag carriers drawing a hard line between elite business class amenities and standard main cabin seating. However, as Porter Airlines aggressively expands its fleet of Embraer E195-E2 jets from coast to coast, the definition of a premium domestic flight has undergone a dramatic transformation. WestJet counters by refining its Boeing 787-9business class and rolling out high-speed Starlink WiFi across its narrowbody fleet, so now, Canadian travelers face two fundamentally different visions of luxury.

Deciding which airline holds the true premium crown depends entirely on whether a passenger values front-of-cabin hard product hardware or an upgraded baseline economy experience. As both carriers vie for market share across transcontinental and transborder routes, comparing their cabin products, seat pitches, and inflight services is more important than ever before booking.

WestJet offers the superior high-end premium product, while Porter Airlines delivers a far more upscale everyday experience for the average passenger. WestJet’s top-tier product is its business class cabin on the 787-9, which features fully lie-flat seats, direct aisle access, premium dining, and dedicated lounge access on long-haul routes. Conversely, Porter does not fly widebody aircraft or offer lie-flat seats, instead focusing on what it markets as an elevated economy experience across its entire fleet.

The fundamental difference lies in how each airline treats the main cabin. As per Seat Maps, Porter’s E195-E2 jets feature a two-by-two seating configuration with no middle seats, complimentary beer and wine served in real glassware, premium Canadian snacks, and fast, free WiFi for every passenger. WestJet’s narrowbody Boeing 737 fleet sticks to a traditional three-by-three layout in economy, where middle seats remain standard and buy-on-board food and drink policies apply.

Ultimately, WestJet wins for long-haul luxury and dedicated premium seating upfront, whereas Porter wins for overall comfort and inflight amenities in the main cabin. For anyone seeking true intercontinental luxury, complete with fully lie-flat suites, direct aisle access, multi-course dining, and dedicated airport lounge access, WestJet’s 787-9 fleet provides a full-service hard product that Porter cannot match. However, for standard domestic economy travel, Porter completely reshapes expectations by removing the dreaded middle seat across its entire E195-E2 fleet.

On narrowbody routes, WestJet’s premium product is WestJet Premium, situated in the forward rows of its 737s. This dedicated cabin features much wider recliner seats in a two-by-two layout, 37 inches to 38 inches (94 centimeters to 97 centimeters) of seat pitch, hot meal choices, and complimentary alcoholic drinks served on multi-hour flights.

Porter takes a different hardware approach with its top fare, PorterReserve. Rather than installing wider business-class seats, PorterReserve utilizes the same two-by-two seat frame found throughout the E195-E2 cabin, but expands seat pitch substantially to 36 inches (91 centimeters) across the first four rows. Instead of a wider chair, PorterReserve is a fully bundled, all-inclusive fare tier that includes fresh meals, pre-mixed cocktails, dedicated airport check-in, priority security screening, early boarding, two free checked bags, and fee-free flight changes.

On shorter domestic hops, PorterReserve frequently delivers comparable legroom and superior soft-product perks at a fraction of the cost of traditional business class. However, on transcontinental flights exceeding four hours, flyers seeking a true widebody recliner or lie-flat bed will find WestJet’s hardware significantly more comfortable.

They are from four Canadian airports. Discover them all here!

Aviation analysts and industry reviewers frequently frame PorterReserve not as a traditional business class, but as an enhanced, all-inclusive economy product. A September 2026 review by Frugal Flyer noted that even though PorterReserve falls short of international long-haul business class standards, citing cold meals served in cardboard packaging and standard seat padding, its price-to-value ratio directly challenges Air Canada’s domestic business class and WestJet Premium. The reviewer concluded that Porter is best understood as an upgraded, hassle-free way to fly economy without surprise add-on fees.

Porter’s strategy of democratizing cabin comfort has earned substantial industry accolades. Passengers voted Porter an APEX Four Star Major Airline, while the carrier also earned USA Today’s Readers’ Choice award for Best Economy Class and was named Skytrax’s Best Regional Airline in North America.

Meanwhile, WestJet continues to defend its premium positioning by expanding its long-haul Dreamliner network across Europe and Asia, operating non-stop routes as long as Calgary International Airport (YYC) to Rome Fiumicino Airport (FCO). WestJet executives emphasize that their two-tier strategy, combining international widebody luxury with a high-density regional fleet, provides the full-service flexibility that global business travelers demand, as reported by AvioRadar.

When compared with Canada's flag carrier, Air Canada, both WestJet and Porter fill distinct operational niches in the domestic and transborder markets. Air Canada’s Signature Class on Boeing 787, 777, and Airbus A330 aircraft remains the traditional benchmark for long-haul business class in North America, featuring private executive pods and extensive Maple Leaf Lounge networks. However, on domestic and transborder narrowbody routes, Air Canada’s standard economy cabin features the same three-by-three seating grid and buy-on-board food service found across WestJet’s 737 fleet.

Against low-cost alternatives like Flair Airlines, Porter and WestJet sit in a completely different tier of reliability and service. Ultra-low-cost carriers strip away all passenger amenities to offer bare-bones transport, whereas Porter elevates the baseline flight experience without charging flag-carrier premium prices. Meanwhile, WestJet approaches its own soft product differentiation by offering a spectrum of products ranging from ultra-basic economy up to widebody transcontinental business suites.

This positioning explains why customer choice varies so much by market segment. For price-sensitive travelers wanting an uncompromised economy flight, Porter beats both Air Canada and WestJet on value. However, for corporate travelers who rely on alliance connections, global lounge access, or international lie-flat seats, traditional network carriers like Air Canada and WestJet are still considered the necessary choice.

Montreal's new $450 million airport, YHU, aims to avoid Mirabel's pitfalls by focusing on domestic convenience rather than international prestige.

It is clear that Porter’s product highlights are compelling, but there are very real and impactful trade-offs that exist, trade-offs that travelers really need to evaluate carefully before booking. Network scale and schedule redundancy are the major factors to keep a close eye on as Porter’s jet fleet and route map, though expanding rapidly across North America, is a fraction of the size of Canada's traditional market leaders. If an aircraft suffers a mechanical delay or severe weather cancellation, WestJet’s broader fleet and dense flight schedules offer far more daily rebooking options to help stranded travelers recover. Passengers on thin Porter routes may face significantly longer wait times for the next available seat during irregular operations.

Rapid network expansion also introduces operational strain that directly impacts schedule reliability. Industry tracking data from Cirium records Porter’s on-time arrival rate trailing competitors at 71.9%, compared to WestJet’s 73.6% on-time performance. In real-world terms, this gap means a higher likelihood of flight delays for passengers working around tight connection windows or strict business itineraries. Combined with Porter’s leaner fleet infrastructure, a single delayed turnaround can trigger compounding schedule slippage throughout the day, whereas WestJet's operational scale lets it manage aircraft swaps and delay buffers more effectively across its main hub channels.

None (Embraer E195-E2 / Dash 8-Q400 only)

2-2 across entire jet fleet (zero middle seats)

Passengers that are accustomed to traditional business-class perks should note that PorterReserve does not grant access to third-party airport lounges. Those seeking quiet terminal spaces or complimentary meals before departure must rely on independent credit card lounge passes or opt for WestJet Premium and Business fares. Additionally, dual-airport cities present routing traps, as Porter operates out of both Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) and Billy Bishop Toronto City Centre Airport (YTZ), meaning travelers need to double-check departure locations to avoid costly airport mix-ups.

The rivalry between WestJet and Porter Airlines in 2026 shows a clear division of passenger priorities across North American skies. If your primary goal is securing a true lie-flat suite on an international flight, or sitting in a wide, dedicated recliner seat with lounge access on a long transcontinental route, WestJet offers the superior hardware product.

However, for short-haul regional routes and transcontinental travel in standard economy, Porter delivers an unmatched base experience. With zero middle seats, free fast Wi-Fi, and an amazing drinks service included for every single passenger, Porter has successfully raised the bar for everyday domestic air travel.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

When choosing between the two Canadian carriers, the best way to make the right choice is to take a closer look at specific aircraft types and total route duration. For quick two-to-three-hour hops, Porter’s standard cabin or PorterReserve fare offers extraordinary overall value. For long-haul intercontinental journeys where seat width and flat-bed rest are paramount, WestJet’s premium cabins will be the definitive choice.

Country singer Jessie James Decker shared video of herself spraying the bare foot of a passenger that had invaded her plane armrest. She holds her nose, takes aim with a small mint-green bottle, and the foot quickly disappears. Then she covers her mouth and laughs. Her Instagram video says, “Someone’s foot smells so bad on the plane.” She asked her followers how they would have handled it. Several suspected she was just messing with her husband, former football player Eric Decker. She refuted that: “Have you seen Eric’s feet? Toeeeee UP.” Jessie James Decker’s airplane video Decker is a country pop singer whose 2017 album Southern Girl City Lights debuted at number one on Billboard’s country albums chart. Her sister is Sydney Rae Bass, whose husband Anthony Bass complained that United Airlines made his pregnant wife clean up their child’s spilled popcorn a few years ago. In April, an American Airlines first class passenger shoved a woman’s feet off their armrest, only to see her put them up on the window. The suggestions in that discussion included spraying cologne. Here Decker puts that into practice. Somehow though this keeps happening? I’d want that foot gone, too. I’d ask the passenger to move it, and get a flight attendant involved if they refused. Some Facebook commenters insist this isn’t the crew’s job. They shouldn’t have to deal with it, and neither should a passenger. Each of us is supposed to contain our bodies within the space of our assigned seats. #6211. What Is A Lifestyle Hotel? The “Cool” Hotel Trend That Means Nothing

It goes without saying that the hospitality industry has a lot of trends. At times there might not actually be much substance to these trends, but the idea is that executives in the industry think certain things are “hot,” and they perceive it to reflect consumer demand.

Along those lines, if you look at trends among the major hotel groups, the concept of “lifestyle hotels” has become incredibly popular. There are an endless number of brands like these that have emerged. I think one logical question is what the term actually means. What makes a property a lifestyle hotel, rather than an… umm, not lifestyle hotel?

I know I’m generally pretty verbose and use a fairly limited vocabulary when it comes to describing things, but that’s intentional. In part, my issue is that many of the descriptors used in marketing, particularly in the travel industry, are so beyond meaningless:

My point is, we’re completely desensitized to useless descriptions of every aspect of the travel experience… unless you’re currently enjoying a seasonal fruit plate served by a private Michelin star chef on a plane, in which case I can’t save you. 😉

Anyway, that brings us to lifestyle hotels, one of the hottest trends in the hotel industry. It’s easy to name brands that claim to be lifestyle hotels — we’re talking Hilton’s Canopy and Curio Collection, Hyatt’s Andaz and Thompson, IHG’s Kimpton and voco, Marriott’s W Hotels and Autograph Collection, etc.

I guess the best way to define a lifestyle hotel would be to step back for a moment, and separate out the two words. Generally a lifestyle brand is a company that sells products by associating them with a specific way of living, set of values, or identities, that customers want to adopt.

A lifestyle hotel is generally defined as a property offering the personalization of an independent boutique hotel, with the attributes of a chain hotel (meaning loyalty, distribution power, etc.). Generally (but not always) these properties have a strong food & beverage or social concept as a core pillar, since that’s a large attribute that can make a hotel popular with a certain guest profile.

The issue with the concept of lifestyle hotels is that hotels can choose how they want to market themselves, and I think some hotels take a “fake it till you make it” approach. If you ask me, the concept of a lifestyle hotel should come down to two factors:

We can of course create all kinds of more specific distinctions, but I think it’s unnecessary. I’ve already written in the past about the concept of “boutique” hotels, another term that means so little. As far as I’m concerned, a lifestyle hotel could be small or big, as the big question is how bustling it is relative to its size.

But this also gets at the issue of how hotel groups choose to label their brands. For example, Marriott labels AC Hotels, Aloft, Autograph Collection, Element, Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, and W Hotels, all as lifestyle brands. From my perspective:

I mean, I live pretty close to a Moxy, and I’ve never thought to myself “hey family, maybe we should go to the Moxy for dinner tonight” (as much as my older son would probably love going somewhere and being able to microwave his own dinner).

So to me, these are the hotels that very much fit into the “fake it until you make it” camp. Like, the major hotel groups want to convince investors and customers that these are somehow something they aren’t. I mean, I’ve also had pleasant stays at AC Hotels properties, and that’s described as “a lifestyle brand that celebrates a new modern aesthetic complemented by a European soul and Spanish roots.” I mean… really?

Hotel groups love to grow and market their lifestyle hotel brands, but I feel like they take a lot of liberties with how they define these. On the most basic level, the idea is supposed to be that lifestyle hotels offer a boutique hotel-style experience, while being associated with one of the major brands.

However, I’d say more accurately, it’s about how much of a “destination” a property is, as that also determines the vibe of the place. I’d love if someone could help me understand just how hotel groups can in good conscience categorize some brands as being lifestyle hotels. Like, how does Marriott include AC Hotels, Autograph Collection, EDITION, and Moxy, all under that same umbrella?

How do you define the lifestyle hotel concept?

I have a personal preference for Lyft, as regular readers know. One of the things that I really like is that they have the best rewards in rideshare. But I didn’t realize things get even more lucrative for business travelers using a Lyft business profile. They have benefits, like:

keeping all of your regular rewards to use on personal or business rides. earning with Lyft’s airline or hotel partners goes up significantly for eligible business travelers. and pocketing 6% – 8% back in Lyft Credits on business profile rides, to use on your own rides later. That’s why it makes sense to sign up for a business account. Bonus, it lets you separate personal and business rides, which makes expense management easier (and you won’t mistakenly apply personal credits to reimbursable trips as I sometimes do by accident). Earn Lyft Credits On Top of Travel Rewards The original idea of a frequent flyer program was that you’d earn rewards on business travel. Your employer pays for a ticket, you benefit personally with your miles. That kept you loyal. This is really the same idea that the airlines pioneered about 45 years ago. When you ride for work, you can get Lyft Credits to use on your own trips later – 6% for standard rides taken with your business profile and 8% for premium, airport, and scheduled business profile rides. And you can do this even while earning with your preferred travel partner, and you earn those points or miles faster than you do with a personal account (where I’ve already been happy with the points-earning). How To Join I already use Lyft for business travel, so enrolling is a no-brainer since it’s fast and free and you accelerate your earnings. This also lets you bill a business card or directly to your employer and it integrates with popular expense tools. Lyft estimates that over half of business travelers forget to take advantage of automatic company expensing, leading to missed rewards and lack of visibility for organizations. Can We Just Appreciate Rideshare For A Moment? For most of my life there was no such thing as rideshare. For a brief time in Austin where I live, the city government chased it away, and I actually had to re-learn how to get to the airport. Now I pull up my Lyft app and I’m frustrated if I see that my driver is six minutes away. Six minutes. That’s my complaint. A stranger is coming to my exact location, in their personal car, because I touched glass. That’s sorcery with seatbelts. It used to be that you had to stand on the curb with your arm out like the Statue of Liberty, just waving at traffic. “Please! Someone! I have money and a destination!” And the taxis would just drive by. Sometimes they’d slow down just enough to let you experience hope before crushing it. You’d make eye contact with the driver. He’d look at you, look through you, and drive right past. And if it rained? You were done. Some cab would blast through a puddle and soak you like you’re Carrie Bradshaw in Sex and the City. Now you press a button and a tiny map shows you a little car cartoon coming toward you. You get in, you get out. Start to finish, it’s frictionless. And to top it off, you even get rewarded for it. Just by using a business profile, you can earn Lyft Credits and extra travel points or miles on rides your company is already paying for. George Clooney said it best in Up In The Air, “I don’t spend a nickel if I can help it unless it somehow benefits my mileage account.” Your company is spending the nickel. You might as well get the miles. Chase's premium business card offers multiple benefits, including useful statement credits and travel perks.

Welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Sapphire Reserve for Business combines premium travel perks with strong earning potential for business owners who spend heavily in some of its bonus categories.

For TPG founder Brian Kelly, the card's earning potential on advertising purchases has been particularly valuable. "The Sapphire Reserve for Business has let me consolidate my spending and keep earning beyond those limits, which is a big deal for growing our TPG brand," he said.

The card earns 3 points per dollar spent on social media and search engine advertising purchases (capped at $1 million in spending each anniversary year beginning Nov. 15), and Brian has also gotten significant value from its travel benefits. He has used The Edit to book luxury hotel stays with on-property perks such as daily breakfast for two and property credits, while also taking advantage of Chase's Points Boost for select hotel and airfare redemptions.

To learn more, read our full review of the Sapphire Reserve for Business.

Apply here: Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business

The Amex Platinum is one of our favorite luxury travel cards thanks to its long list of useful benefits, including airport lounge access and valuable statement credits.

Welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Why we love it: TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak finds solid value in the Amex Platinum's benefits. Specifically, Olivia enjoys receiving the up to $155 Walmart+ statement credit per calendar year (up to $12.95 monthly, plus applicable taxes) that covers the cost of a monthly membership when paying with the Amex Platinum (on one membership, subject to auto-renewal; Plus Ups excluded).

Walmart+ includes a complimentary Paramount+ subscription (separate enrollment is required), which allows her to avoid paying out of pocket for the streaming service.

She also uses the card's up to $300 Lululemon statement credit per calendar year at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online (allocated as up to $75 per quarter) and up to $400 Resy statement credit per calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter; simply pay with your Amex Platinum at an eligible U.S. Resy restaurant; no reservation is required).

To learn more, read our full review of the American Express Platinum.

The Capital One Venture Rewards is a straightforward travel rewards card that earns at least 2 miles per dollar on every purchase and gives cardholders access to Capital One's airline and hotel transfer partners.

Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, receive a $300 credit to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year upon account opening.

Why we love it: The Venture Rewards offers a simple earning structure and flexible redemption options for a reasonable $95 annual fee.

Cardholders earn at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, so there's no need to keep track of bonus categories. For potentially greater value, you can transfer your miles to Capital One's airline and hotel partners.

TPG points and loyalty lead writer Katie Genter has held the Venture Rewards for years and values it for many of the same reasons. "I like the Venture's straightforward earning structure, and the fact that it earns versatile yet valuable Capital One miles," she said.

The current offer is particularly appealing because the $300 Capital One Travel credit comes on top of the 75,000-mile bonus, making an already strong offer even more rewarding in the first year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards.

The United Explorer is a solid option for travelers who fly United several times a year and want valuable airline perks without paying a premium annual fee.

Why we love it: The Explorer offers several useful United benefits, including a free first checked bag for the cardmember and one companion (when the flight is purchased with the card), priority boarding and two United Club one-time passes each cardholder year.

TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak has held the Explorer for years and particularly appreciates how easy it is to get value from the card's United-specific benefits.

"The biggest reason I tout the Explorer as often as I do is because of how easy it is to get meaningful value from it without needing to use merchant credits that may not fit your spending habits," she said.

With a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150), the Explorer could be particularly appealing to travelers who regularly check bags or use United Club access.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer Card.

The Hilton Honors Aspire is a premium hotel card that offers valuable benefits for travelers who regularly stay at Hilton properties.

Welcome offer: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

Why we love it: The Aspire offers automatic Hilton Honors Diamond status, an annual free night reward and up to $400 in statement credits for eligible Hilton resort purchases each calendar year (up to $200 biannually).

For Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site strategy, the free night reward and resort credits are among her favorite credit card benefits. Both she and her husband hold the Aspire, allowing them to take advantage of two sets of these benefits each year.

The card's perks can help offset the card's $550 annual fee, particularly for travelers who can redeem their free night rewards at high-end Hilton properties.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Aspire.

The United Gateway is an entry-level United credit card that lets travelers earn MileagePlus miles without paying an annual fee.

Welcome offer: Earn up to 50,000 bonus miles: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Why we love it: The Gateway offers a straightforward way to earn United miles on everyday purchases while avoiding an annual fee. It's a strong option for occasional United flyers who want to build their MileagePlus balances but don't need the more extensive travel benefits of the airline's higher-tier cards.

TPG credit card writer Becky Pokora appreciates the card's everyday earning opportunities: "I keep my card linked to my toll road and Parkmobile accounts, since it earns extra miles on local transit and commuting charges and defines those categories broadly," she said.

Becky also uses the card for inflight purchases to receive a 25% statement credit on eligible purchases, another perk that adds value without an annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Gateway Card.

These offers can help you boost your transferable points and miles balance or unlock meaningful discounts on your next trip.

As always, be sure to factor in each issuer's unique set of application restrictions and ensure you can meet any spending requirements to earn the bonus.

But with so much value on the table, you won't want to miss out on adding one of these top credit cards (and its bonus) to your wallet.

#6207. How Perth Easily Became Australia's Gateway To Europe

Australian travelers bound for Europe have always had to face a two-stage journey, with a domestic transcontinental flight to an east-coast hub, followed by a long-haul connection through the Middle East or Southeast Asia. There is one location that bucks this trend, that being Perth. Sitting nearly 2,000 miles (3,218 km) closer to London than Sydney, quietly positioned Western Australia as the nation's natural international springboard, the Western Australian city has become the main entry point for non-stop flights to continental Europe.

That transformation did not happen by accident; it came as a result of a fundamental realignment of airline fleet strategies, airport infrastructure investments, and international route rights. Using advanced long-range twin-engine aircraft, Qantas turned Perth International Airport (PER) into a high-yield international hub. But as airspace disruptions and competing long-haul technologies emerge, how long can Western Australia maintain its exclusive hold as Australia's direct bridge to Europe?

Perth became Australia’s gateway to Europe due to its location, as the vast distance between the southern continent and European airspace is within the maximum range limits of modern twin-engine airliners. In March 2018, Qantas launched its historic 9,010-mile (14,499 km) Perth to London Heathrow Airport(LHR) route using a 236-seat Boeing 787-9, as covered by Fortune. Flying directly out of Western Australia cuts three to four hours off the total travel time compared to departing from Sydney or Melbourne Airport(MEL), which therefore removes the traditional intermediate stopover in Singapore Changi Airport (SIN), Dubai International Airport(DXB), or Doha Hamad International Airport(DOH).

According to reporting from The Points Guy, that single route showed that non-stop ultra-long-haul flights between Australia and Europe were not only technically feasible, but exceptionally profitable. The success of the London service encouraged Qantas and local state planners to expand the Perth hub, eventually leading to the launch of Perth– Rome Fiumicino Airport(FCO) in June 2022, the first direct flight connecting Australia with continental Europe, and a subsequent seasonal non-stop service to Paris Charles De Gaulle Airport(CDG).

As highlighted in Travel Weekly, Qantas confirmed that 2026 would be its biggest year yet for Western Australia, adding nearly 300,000 seats between Perth and London, Paris, and Rome. In fact, the Perth–Rome route alone gained 44 extra flights and close to 10,000 more inbound seats between May and October 2026, as per the Government Of Western Australia. This massive expansion reinforced Western Australia's unique status as the only Australian state offering direct, non-stop passenger services into the European continent.

Supporting high-yield international transit traffic meant Perth Airport and Qantas had to overcome the separation between domestic and international terminals. Traditionally, passengers connecting from Melbourne, Sydney, or Brisbane had to land at the domestic terminal precinct and transfer across the airfield to the international terminal, creating a friction-filled connection experience. To resolve this, Qantas negotiated a custom arrangement to process international customs and immigration directly within its domestic Terminal 3 and 4 wing, as reported by MTA Travel.

The temporary operational fix laid the groundwork for Perth Airport’s massive "One Airport" consolidation program. According to an official media statement from the Government of Western Australia, WA Premier Roger Cook stated that these expanded international connections "cement WA's status as the gateway to Australia from Europe", noting that over 20 non-stop international routes now operate out of Perth. This multi-billion-dollar infrastructure effort aims to consolidate all domestic and international flights into a unified central terminal precinct, drastically reducing transfer friction for connecting passengers.

As well as the European routes, Qantas expanded Perth's network horizon even further by adding non-stop flights from Perth to Johannesburg Airport(JNB) and Auckland Airport(AKL) starting in December 2025. Connecting trans-Tasman, African, and European corridors through a single hub meant that Perth Airport could change its identity from a regional destination into a major global transit nexus. However, just as Perth was solidifying its status as an unshakeable aviation crossroads, major geopolitical shifts halfway across the globe put its route network to a tough operational test.

A closer look at why Qantas made adjustment to one of the world's longest non-stop flights

Geopolitical conflicts across the Middle East have caused major challenges for global air corridors, forcing international airlines to navigate closed or restricted airspace over Iran, Iraq, and the Levant region. For traditional Gulf mega-carriers operating out of hubs like Dubai, Doha, and Abu Dhabi, flight paths faced rerouting or temporary operational halts. As reported by Aerospace Global News, this systemic disruption created an unprecedented surge in demand for alternative routes linking Australia directly to Europe. Travelers who previously opted for a Middle East transfer sought out Qantas's direct services out of Western Australia to avoid the volatile airspace altogether.

However, the unforgiving flight-planning realities of ultra-long-haul aviation meant that Qantas faced its own operational complications. As highlighted in coverage by Simple Flying, westbound headwinds combined with strict airspace avoidance protocols forced Qantas to adjust its flagship outbound flights. Outbound services from Perth to London and Sydney to Paris via Perth were rerouted through Singapore Changi for technical refueling stops, though the inbound flights from London and Paris back to Perth continued to operate non-stop.

During these operational changes, Perth–Rome stood out as a critical non-stop survivor. In order to capture redirected European demand, Qantas boosted Perth–Rome services from four weekly flights to daily operations, adding over 1,400 seats per week to the continent during peak seasons. Such tactical network shifts brought to center stage both the strategic resilience and the delicate operational vulnerability of running ultra-long-haul corridors out of Western Australia.

Operating commercial non-stop sectors exceeding 8,000 miles (12,874 km) is exactly where operational factors need to be monitored closely. Payload capacity, fuel burn, and takeoff weight limits massively affect the viability of the flight, and so a balance needs to be achieved. The 787-9 aircraft assigned to Qantas’s long-haul Perth operations feature a custom passenger configuration of just 236 seats, significantly lower than the standard high-density layouts deployed by international competitors. Restricting cabin capacity reduces total payload weight, allowing the twin-engine widebody to carry the massive fuel load required for a 17-hour block time.

Every additional seat, cargo pallet, or gallon of jet fuel alters the aircraft's takeoff performance, particularly during warm Australian summer months. When strong winter jet streams push against westbound aircraft over the Indian Ocean, flight planning managers rigorously weigh passenger counts against fuel reserves. If headwind components exceed baseline estimates, the aircraft risks exceeding its Maximum Takeoff Weight (MTOW) or infringing strict Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards (ETOPS) margins.

The constraints here explain why Qantas relies on premium-heavy cabin configurations and elevated ticket yields to make these non-stop routes viable. Despite this, as airframe technologies advance, Perth's hard-won geographic monopoly faces a threat from within Qantas’s own future fleet commitments.

Qantas shakes up its international network to offer more flights to Europe via Singapore.

The long-term outlook for Perth as Australia's main European gateway faces a major test from Qantas's flagship ultra-long-haul initiative, Project Sunrise. Designed to connect Sydney and Melbourne directly to London Heathrow and New York non-stop using ultra-long-range Airbus A350-1000ULR aircraft, Project Sunrise will completely remove the need for an intermediate domestic transit stop in Western Australia.

Once direct non-stop flights from the East Coast launch, a significant portion of high-yield corporate travelers who currently route through Perth will opt for point-to-point non-stop services from Sydney or Melbourne. According to reporting by The Points Guy, Project Sunrise specifically targets high-yield travelers on Australia's busiest transcontinental corridors, potentially diverting transit traffic away from Western Australia’s hub.

Replacing Perth is not quite the plan, as Qantas plans to position the two operations as complementary long-haul networks. While Project Sunrise caters to premium demand from Australia's largest financial centers on the east coast, Perth will continue serving as a regional springboard, capturing origin-and-destination demand across Western Australia, trans-Tasman feeder traffic, and routes to Southern Africa.

Perth's transformation into Australia's primary direct gateway to Europe is really something special, something that quite often gets overlooked in the global aviation world. Non-stop ultra-long-haul routes could succeed using fuel-efficient twin-engine widebodies, so Qantas and Perth Airport were able to jointly morph international travel patterns across the Southern Hemisphere.

The long-term test for Western Australia will be maintaining its route volume as Project Sunrise aircraft enter service and direct east-coast routes come online. Continued investment in terminal consolidation under Perth Airport’s "One Airport" masterplan, combined with scheduled route restorations, including Qantas returning the Perth–London sector to a full non-stop rotation, are really what will determine whether Perth retains its dominance as a transit hub.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Airspace restrictions and jet fuel economics are still highly volatile, but Western Australia's geographic location is an unshakable natural asset. Perth was able to make direct connections from Australia to the other side of the world possible, so even if Project Sunrise takes away its lead, we still have Perth to thank for opening up one of the longest direct route selections in the world.

#6206. Marriott Earnings Call: New Upgrade List Encourages Elites To Pay For Better Rooms—But Puts Its Credit Card Cash Cow At Risk

Marriott earned $794 million in the third quarter, up from $728 million a year ago. They’re doing well. At the same time, I’ve been covering reports of layoffs in the customer service teams guests turn to when hotels won’t honor benefits. And on their earnings call, Marriott explained that its new elite upgrade list is being designed to preserve owners’ ability to sell upgrades. The company is getting better at monetizing Bonvoy. More than half its fee growth came from credit cards. But they’re spending down the trust that makes the program worth something in the first place. The hotel business has been good, outside of pockets like the Mideast. Marriott’s revenue per available room rose 6.5%. Adjusted earnings per share rose from $2.47 to $3.02, beating the $2.84 analysts expected. Marriott’s quarterly filing identifies $68 million in additional credit card fees compared with the same quarter last year. More than half of the increase in franchise fees comes from cards. Third Quarter Fee Growth   Increase   Share From Higher Card Fees Franchise fees   $131 million   52% Total gross fees   $184 million   37% I’ve covered owners’ unhappiness with these economics. Fifty-one owners representing about 1,000 hotels demanded better compensation for award stays. They’re supplying the rooms, Marriott sells them at a discount to Chase and American Express customers. The basic hotel loyalty bargain is a loop. Hotels pay into a program that rewards guests for stays. Those guests redeem points for more stays. Owners supply discounted award nights in exchange for a program that encourages customers to choose their hotels. A vacant room is cheap to give away. When an award guest doesn’t displace a paying customer, the hotel’s cost is mostly cleaning, utilities and whatever benefits it provides. Deep discounts make sense. But Marriott selling the points through Chase and American Express, using access to those discounted nights to monetize the owners’ inventory, infuriates some of them. As I’ve explained about bank payments for rewards, Marriott’s reported card fees aren’t everything the banks pay. Some money funds points and benefits. Some pays Marriott for licensing its brand and customer access. On the earnings call, Marriott pointed to the ways they’re appeasing owners: lower fees for Bonvoy higher reimbursement on high-demand award nights more flexible renovation requirements (letting owners allow the product to slip) a guest recommendation incentive. Marriott discussed its new upgrade lists. I covered the beta last month. Members can see their place in line and an estimate of upgrades matching their reservation. CEO Anthony Capuano told investors the feature would provide that visibility “while still preserving premium room upsell opportunities for our owners.” Showing you a position on a list doesn’t commit a room to you. A hotel can keep selling premium rooms while guests wait for complimentary upgrades. The later it commits the room, the longer it has to find someone willing to pay. Marriott hasn’t explained the beta’s inventory or clearance rules. They’re promising more visibility, but they aren’t saying hotels will release more rooms or confirm upgrades earlier. People who are lower on the list – and therefore less likely to get a free upgrade – become motivated to buy the upsell. Which, in turn, means fewer upgrade rooms available even at the top of the list. I’ve already described where Marriott’s technology investment is headed: selling room attributes and extras that guests used to receive as part of their stay or status. Better views, room locations and upgrades are going to become new opportunities for revenue generation. Selling a premium room is perfectly reasonable. But Bonvoy also encourages guests to concentrate their stays and spending to earn upgrades. And they’ll sell those same upgrades back to lower-tier elites for tens of dollars – prioritizing minor ducats over long-term value. Meanwhile, Capuano trumpeted 309 million Bonvoy members. I’m amazed anyone keeps repeating these enrollment numbers seriously. It means a guest signed up to get a lower (member) room rate. That tells us they wanted to pay less for the reservation they were already making. It says nothing about interest in Bonvoy or continued engagement. And the numbers are large because Marriott has a lot of hotels and rooms. I’ve reported on employees signing guests up who don’t even know about it, alongside hotel incentives worth as much as $10,000 a month for enrollment performance. Marriott intentionally does not share active members When I wrote about Chris Buckner taking over Bonvoy, I argued that his biggest opportunity was getting hotels to deliver the benefits members had already earned. Marriott’s business depends on guests starting their hotel search with Marriott. The brand is supposed to stand for a consistent product, and Bonvoy is supposed to make the brand sticky. That’s what lets Marriott deliver customers to owners as “leads” and charge for access to them. The reservation system doesn’t have value to sell to owners if guests stop trusting the hotels it displays. An individual owner can save money by denying breakfast or an upgrade. The damage gets spread across the whole portfolio. That hotel benefits from shirking on the program, while the program loses value. That’s why Marriott is supposed to enforce its promises. Yet they rarely seem to! I covered a breakfast dispute where the hotel closed the guest’s case seven times before finally paying the $100 benefit guarantee the guest was clearly due. In Marriott’s system, the hotel becomes the judge of complaints against it. . At the same time, I’ve been covering reports of layoffs in the customer service teams guests turn to when hotels won’t honor benefits. And on their earnings call, Marriott explained that its new elite upgrade list is being designed to preserve owners’ ability to sell upgrades.

The company is getting better at monetizing Bonvoy. More than half its fee growth came from credit cards. But they’re spending down the trust that makes the program worth something in the first place.

As I’ve explained about bank payments for rewards, Marriott’s reported card fees aren’t everything the banks pay. Some money funds points and benefits. Some pays Marriott for licensing its brand and customer access.

On the earnings call, Marriott pointed to the ways they’re appeasing owners: lower fees for Bonvoy higher reimbursement on high-demand award nights more flexible renovation requirements (letting owners allow the product to slip) a guest recommendation incentive. Marriott discussed its new upgrade lists. I covered the beta last month. Members can see their place in line and an estimate of upgrades matching their reservation. CEO Anthony Capuano told investors the feature would provide that visibility “while still preserving premium room upsell opportunities for our owners.” Showing you a position on a list doesn’t commit a room to you. A hotel can keep selling premium rooms while guests wait for complimentary upgrades. The later it commits the room, the longer it has to find someone willing to pay. Marriott hasn’t explained the beta’s inventory or clearance rules. They’re promising more visibility, but they aren’t saying hotels will release more rooms or confirm upgrades earlier. People who are lower on the list – and therefore less likely to get a free upgrade – become motivated to buy the upsell. Which, in turn, means fewer upgrade rooms available even at the top of the list. I’ve already described where Marriott’s technology investment is headed: selling room attributes and extras that guests used to receive as part of their stay or status. Better views, room locations and upgrades are going to become new opportunities for revenue generation. Selling a premium room is perfectly reasonable. But Bonvoy also encourages guests to concentrate their stays and spending to earn upgrades. And they’ll sell those same upgrades back to lower-tier elites for tens of dollars – prioritizing minor ducats over long-term value. Meanwhile, Capuano trumpeted 309 million Bonvoy members. I’m amazed anyone keeps repeating these enrollment numbers seriously. It means a guest signed up to get a lower (member) room rate. That tells us they wanted to pay less for the reservation they were already making. It says nothing about interest in Bonvoy or continued engagement. And the numbers are large because Marriott has a lot of hotels and rooms. I’ve reported on employees signing guests up who don’t even know about it, alongside hotel incentives worth as much as $10,000 a month for enrollment performance. Marriott intentionally does not share active members When I wrote about Chris Buckner taking over Bonvoy, I argued that his biggest opportunity was getting hotels to deliver the benefits members had already earned. Marriott’s business depends on guests starting their hotel search with Marriott. The brand is supposed to stand for a consistent product, and Bonvoy is supposed to make the brand sticky. That’s what lets Marriott deliver customers to owners as “leads” and charge for access to them. The reservation system doesn’t have value to sell to owners if guests stop trusting the hotels it displays. An individual owner can save money by denying breakfast or an upgrade. The damage gets spread across the whole portfolio. That hotel benefits from shirking on the program, while the program loses value. That’s why Marriott is supposed to enforce its promises. Yet they rarely seem to! I covered a breakfast dispute where the hotel closed the guest’s case seven times before finally paying the $100 benefit guarantee the guest was clearly due. In Marriott’s system, the hotel becomes the judge of complaints against it. . So, they learned from Delta’s earnings calls to not literally say the quiet part out loud and be explicitly evil. (“We’re gonna price-gouge the sh*t outta our customers!”) Huh. Wild.

At many properties, you need to have a Bonvoy number to get complimentary internet. There would be less Bonvoy members if they didn’t do this.

Also, always use a VPN, so that Bonvoy isn’t building a profile on your internet history.

I may be one of the most infrequent travelers, but I still remember the moments I signed on encouraged by desk staff to SPG when staying at the Sheraton Boston. I was immediately upgraded to a mini suite and got take out from the Kon TIki off the lobby and enjoyed every minute of my stay. What I lack in travel (due to work, caregiving, and health issues of my own) I make up for in loyalty and I never voted as the Shareholder I became based on my visits since a teen to the new (then) Sheraton Toronto. I am devastated by the ignorance of one of the most valued aspects imo of Marriott buying out Starwood, which I, as a tiny shareholder did not endorse. Heartbreaking that they have managed to destroy what was such a wonderful program. THe stupidity was obvious when they trashed all of our SPG numbers and did not provide new membership cards, not to mention how imo the related AMEX card art was well, I was going to say ugly, but I will say it is unappealing.

Unfortunately that is the norm in the US! Screw the customer! Let the hotel deny anything they want. I don’t expect any upgrade as a Platinum in the US. My number one complaint is breakfast in a High-end Marriott ! When you pay 800-1K or more? You don’t want continental breakfast! You don’t want them to act like they are doing you a favor giving you a donut! Most of all after you have spent all that money becoming so called the customer they want……then Marriot do as little as they can for that loyalty

I used to play a game called Roller Coaster Tycoon. One time I built an amusement park, where nobody could leave. At first it worked great. Then the customers became more and more unhappy, and no new people came to my amusement park.

More seriously, goodwill is an asset. Over the short run, you can increase profits by monetizing assets. However, over the long run, that will cause the goodwill to depreciate significantly. Famous brands that have no value any more are everywhere.

I am lifetime Platinum (Titanium currently). However, Marriott’s tricky app (in terms of pricing and cancellation date) (as I commented previously), removal of the ability to add guests, and other unfriendly acts are causing me to book elsewhere often.

For example, I am planning to meet my girlfriend near LAX. The LAX Marriott would normally be a good choice. However, we are flying in on different itineraries. If my plane is delayed, she won’t be able to check in. Going to book elsewhere.

As a Starwood transfer and current Marriott Lifetime Titanium (1700+ nights) I’m very disappointed with Marriott/Bonvoy. One problem might be that Marriott gives away upper tier status just by holding credit cards. When you can reach upper tier status basically just by holding credit cards, of course that status is going to be worthless.

I actually just reread Gary’s “Marriott Names A New Bonvoy Boss From JetBlue And The Points Guy—Will He Make Hotels Honor Your Benefits?” that he linked to above. It was a pretty good read. I am at the point where I do not expect any of the benefits to be honored. Enough said.

The whole craziness with Marriott and its ongoing process of nickel and diming its customers who buy into its “loyalty” program (Bonvoy) reminds me quite a bit of the “Master of the House” scene in the musical “Les Miserables” in which the innkeeper continually gouges and shortchanges his guests (with unexpected extra charges for everything) … and publicly brags about it. What Marriott does (and increasingly other so-called hospitality companies do) is at best shameful. Marriott and the others are selling you are for the most part illusions and wishful thinking for your blind “loyalty.”

The visible list mostly tells lower tier elites their odds. That’s exactly the moment the upsell starts to look tempting. Paying makes sense when the trip really needs the bigger room, a family stay or an anniversary, or when the paid upgrade is a small add on to the standard rate. If it’s just nice to have, Platinum and above can still sit on the list and see what clears.

The hotel’s own site or Google Hotels will show what that suite category costs booked outright for the same dates. FWIW that same Marriott can also price diff depending on which country you search from, since inventory and rates vary by market. Free tools like Arbitrica check it from around 195 countries and find kind of the lowest price in the world, which tells you fast whether the upsell is a deal. Then decide whether to pay now or gamble on the list

Marriott now views engaged loyalty members as suckers and adversaries. I’m lifetime platinum but generally tend to avoid their hotels.

#6205. Southwest Premier Business Card Review: Is The $149 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card is the more basic of the two Southwest business cards. This card has a $149 annual fee, and gets you a handful of valuable benefits when you fly Southwest, including complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating within 48 hours of departure and a free checked bag, among other things.

If you fly Southwest at least a few times a year and you qualify for a small business credit card, the Southwest Premier Business Card is worth considering. It’s worth an extra close look right now, because now is your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the airline’s valuable Companion Pass benefit. I’ll get into all that and more below in my comprehensive Southwest Premier Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card

Before getting into the Southwest Premier Business Card in detail, let’s take a broader look at the card’s main features:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Premier Business Card:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is Southwest’s entry-level business credit card. Let’s take a look at the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and annual fee, given that these are factors that many people consider when applying for a card.

The Southwest Premier Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each, as that’s roughly the rate at which you can redeem points toward flights. So by my valuation, 60,000 Rapid Rewards points are worth ~$720.

While this is a decent welcome offer, let me note that we’ve seen bigger limited time welcome offers in the past. So if you’re primarily after the best welcome offer, it could make sense to wait to apply.

The welcome bonus on the Southwest Premier Business Card isn’t available to those who currently have this card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), or any personal Southwest credit card.

Also remember Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, apply. With the 5/24 rule, you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the last 24 months. However, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a $149 annual fee. There’s no cost to add additional users to the card. You can set individual spending limits for additional cards, and you can earn points on their spending.

The Southwest Premier Business Card doesn’t charge any foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about racking up extra charges.

Obviously the rewards structure is an important factor to consider when applying for a credit card. So how does the Southwest Premier Business Card do on that front? In addition to offering bonus points in select spending categories, the card also offers the ability to earn status through spending, so let’s cover those details.

As far as the rewards structure goes, the Southwest Premier Business Card offers:

While these are some good bonus categories, I wouldn’t consider this to be an industry-leading rewards structure — there are better cards for airfare spending, and better cards for everyday spending.

Based on my valuation of Southwest points at 1.2 cents each, using the Southwest Premier Business Card to book Southwest flights gets you a 3.6% return on spending, while the 2x and 1x categories get you 2.4% and 1.2% returns on spending, respectively.

Spending on the Southwest Premier Business Card can count toward A-List elite status. Specifically, through the end of 2026 you can earn 2,000 Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward A-List for every $5,000 you spend on the card. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on the card will earn one TQP.

A-List status ordinarily requires 35,000 TQPs per year, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

However, Southwest has announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status. Earning it will require 35,000 TQPs (unchanged) or 25 qualifying flights (up from 20 today).

Personally I probably wouldn’t spend that much money on a credit card to earn A-List status, but for some people this could prove to be worthwhile, especially if you’re close to earning A-List status otherwise.

One of the very best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With Southwest Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket), and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal, and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest. The pass is valid for the rest of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the following full year, so the earlier in the year you earn it, the more it’s worth.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, though, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Business Card; it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that points from the current welcome bonus offer do count toward Companion Pass qualification for the rest of 2026 and through 2027, per Chase’s offer details, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a solid welcome bonus that’s especially valuable now that it’s your last chance to earn it and have it count toward the Companion Pass, but that’s not the only reason to consider this card. There are also several ongoing perks that can make your experience flying Southwest a little more comfortable.

One major ongoing perk of the Southwest Premier Business Card is that you earn 6,000 Rapid Rewards bonus points on your account anniversary every year. As mentioned above, I value Rapid Rewards points at around 1.2 cents each, so to me, that’s like $72 worth of value annually.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation.

If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can help you recoup the annual fee. For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way, so you could save $90 on a roundtrip flight. With two roundtrip flights with checked bags in a year, that already cancels out the $149 annual fee.

As a Southwest Premier Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat within 48 hours prior to departure, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight.

The Southwest Premier Business Card also gets you a 15% promo code each year on your account anniversary. You can use this to score a 15% discount on a Southwest flight, excluding Basic fares. This perk is another nice way the card can save you money when flying Southwest, especially if you book cash tickets in addition to award flights at least once a year.

Southwest Premier Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. This perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers 25% savings on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases on Southwest. Just charge your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for 25% of the purchase total, which should appear within two billing cycles.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a great welcome bonus, and the $149 annual fee can be largely offset by the 6,000 anniversary bonus points and other benefits. The welcome bonus can also go a long way toward earning the Companion Pass, which is all the more reason to get the card now before this opportunity ends.

That said, I don’t necessarily think the Southwest Premier Business Card is a great pick for everyone. If you’re not loyal to Southwest or you split flying across multiple airlines, it’s probably not the best card for you. And if you want flexible points that you can redeem with a variety of airlines and hotels, it could also be best to skip this card.

First, let me compare it to the more premium Southwest Performance Business Card, then I’ll share the points currency I recommend earning instead if you’re mainly concerned with booking award flights on Southwest, not extra perks with the airline.

The Southwest Performance Business Card (learn more) is the more premium sibling of the Southwest Premier Business Card. Overall it comes with more benefits — and in some cases enhanced versions of the same perks on the Southwest Premier Business Card.

Here’s a quick overview of how the Southwest business credit cards compare:

The extra 3,000 anniversary points are worth $36 by my valuation, so you’d need roughly $9,500 in Southwest spending for the extra point per dollar to cover the rest of the $150 fee difference, before counting the seating and Global Entry perks.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and you want as many perks and points as possible, the Southwest Performance Business Card could be worth the higher annual fee.

If your goal is to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points, but you don’t actually plan on earning the Companion Pass or Southwest status, there’s a much faster way to earn those points.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. You can earn points at a much faster rate with the following business cards:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is a good entry-level Southwest Airlines business credit card with a nice welcome bonus. The current bonus can earn you a lot of travel on Southwest, and can even help you earn Companion Pass — but only if you earn the bonus under the current offer, before the 2027 program changes take effect.

This card is definitely worth considering, though the only other consideration is that I think it could be worth paying the premium for the Southwest Performance Business Card, which has better ongoing perks. And earning Ultimate Rewards points with a Chase credit card could also make more sense unless you really value the Southwest-specific benefits.

Which Southwest business credit card do you prefer?

#6203. Oneworld Explains The Money Behind Your Lounge Access—And Why Credit Cards Help Decide Where Airlines Fly

Historically, if I used Royal Jordanian status to enter an American Airlines lounge while flying American, Royal Jordanian didn’t get a bill. American was carrying me and bore the lounge cost. In a new interview, oneworld’s commercial chief describes a payment model that sounds like that arrangement may still apply, despite reporting that says the rules changed. Who pays for your lounge visit helps explain why airline alliances are so difficult to run. The airline that gives you status, the one selling you a ticket, and the one providing your benefits can all be different. Each wants the customer and the revenue, and they have to agree on who picks up the costs. Roger Blackburn, oneworld’s Vice President of Commercial and Loyalty, and Gilbert Ott, its Director of Loyalty (and former blogger of God Save the Points), talk about how this works in an unusually candid interview. It’s essentially herding cats, with airlines that compete for the same customers promising to take care of each other’s passengers. Blackburn explains that a lounge hosting another airline’s passenger gets paid by: …the airline who’s … lifting that customer out of the station. At least that’s how our model works. One Mile at a Time has said its understanding is that this changed, and that the program providing status now pays when status is the reason someone gets in. This affects the economics of status matches, for instance. An airline offering status to someone who mostly flies its partners has a very different cost calculation if it’s getting a bill for every lounge visit. The lack of billing was also a limiting factor on offering status matches (confined to a formula relative to the total size of the elite pool). Blackburn describes the lounge operator as delighted to have another airline’s passenger because they’re getting paid. That true when there are empty seats. When the lounge is full, another paid visit can make the experience worse for the airline’s own customers. I’ve written about American’s lounge visits growing several times as fast as its passenger traffic. Better lounges encourage more people to use them, and to stay longer. Improving the product creates demand for more space. That’s also why Blackburn’s explanation of where oneworld builds its own lounges is helpful. They want airports served by enough member airlines to keep a lounge busy across the day. One airline might struggle to justify the rent and staffing for a single daily departure. Several airlines with departures at different times can share a better facility. Delhi and Mumbai come up in the conversation, and Blackburn hopes to have more lounge news “fairly soon.” The banks competing for that space also help pay for the airlines’ products. Ott argues that credit card and loyalty revenue supports better lounges, seats, food and inflight connectivity. He’s largely right, and the case goes further: credit cards support more flights. An airline becomes more attractive to cardmembers when it flies where they need to go. It also needs destinations they want to redeem their miles for. Delta has explicitly connected its growth in Austin and Raleigh with acquiring American Express card customers. A flight that looks weak based only on ticket revenue might make sense once you count the card spending it helps generate. As I discussed in my recent piece on Scott Kirby and credit card economics, a customer might choose an airline’s card because its Chicago schedule works for their business travel, then redeem the miles for Hawaii. Assign all the card revenue to Hawaii and you can end up cutting the flights that made someone want your card in the first place. A better seat and lounge help sell that relationship, too. And an alliance makes the card more useful by offering places to spend miles that the airline doesn’t fly to itself. Of course airlines can manage this badly. Sell more miles while planes are full, without making enough desirable award seats available, and customers wind up with growing balances they struggle to use. Sell more lounge access without adding enough capacity and the customer gets a line at the door. The alliance has to get its members to participate in making those benefits valuable. Asked whether oneworld should set minimum protections around changes to earning, status qualification and award availability, Ott describes the programs as largely sovereign and emphasizes a spirit of cooperation. Asked how much say the alliance has over the number of award seats a member releases, he calls it a collaborative process. I’d put it a different way: an alliance trying to influence airlines is pushing on a string. It’s the problem I’ve written about with airlines holding back their best awards from partners. They want to offer their members access to everyone else’s seats. But making their own best seats available can benefit another airline’s credit card business, while keeping those seats for their own members can help sell their own miles. Ott makes the case that a redemption can introduce someone to an airline and turn them into a valuable customer. That’s true as far as it goes, but those seats have an opportunity cost and getting the airline with the seat to value that speculative future business enough to release it (for a foreign customer who might not travel with them often and probably won’t take their credit card) can be a challenge. So can getting the partner buying the award seat to pay enough to make that worthwhile. Blackburn says oneworld is improving how quickly miles reach accounts following a flight across the alliance, with everyone expected on a new standard by the end of the year. He also says oneworld’s earlier artificial intelligence round the world booking assistant is gone, despite earlier claims of a fivefold increase in booking conversions. The interview returns to the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September, where I spoke about how artificial intelligence gives customers better tools to choose rewards programs. (The summit photo below is courtesy of oneworld.) Ott mentions verifying elite status without relying on screenshots that someone can easily manipulate. I saw a presentation at the summit for a product that was basically Plaid for airline status: the customer logged into their existing airline account to demonstrate their status to another company. I questioned whether airlines would allow that access to their systems. Topics on this pageAirline alliance stability based on dynamic cooperative game theoryAirport loungeLoyalty programOneworldAmerican AirlinesAmerican ExpressChicagoDelhiDelta Air LinesGodHawaiiMumbaiRaleighRoyal JordanianScott Kirby+11 more More From View from the Wing

Who pays for your lounge visit helps explain why airline alliances are so difficult to run. The airline that gives you status, the one selling you a ticket, and the one providing your benefits can all be different. Each wants the customer and the revenue, and they have to agree on who picks up the costs.

Roger Blackburn, oneworld’s Vice President of Commercial and Loyalty, and Gilbert Ott, its Director of Loyalty (and former blogger of God Save the Points), talk about how this works in an unusually candid interview. It’s essentially herding cats, with airlines that compete for the same customers promising to take care of each other’s passengers.

Blackburn explains that a lounge hosting another airline’s passenger gets paid by:

…the airline who’s … lifting that customer out of the station. At least that’s how our model works.

One Mile at a Time has said its understanding is that this changed, and that the program providing status now pays when status is the reason someone gets in.

This affects the economics of status matches, for instance. An airline offering status to someone who mostly flies its partners has a very different cost calculation if it’s getting a bill for every lounge visit. The lack of billing was also a limiting factor on offering status matches (confined to a formula relative to the total size of the elite pool).

Blackburn describes the lounge operator as delighted to have another airline’s passenger because they’re getting paid. That true when there are empty seats. When the lounge is full, another paid visit can make the experience worse for the airline’s own customers.

I’ve written about American’s lounge visits growing several times as fast as its passenger traffic. Better lounges encourage more people to use them, and to stay longer. Improving the product creates demand for more space.

That’s also why Blackburn’s explanation of where oneworld builds its own lounges is helpful. They want airports served by enough member airlines to keep a lounge busy across the day. One airline might struggle to justify the rent and staffing for a single daily departure. Several airlines with departures at different times can share a better facility. Delhi and Mumbai come up in the conversation, and Blackburn hopes to have more lounge news “fairly soon.”

The banks competing for that space also help pay for the airlines’ products. Ott argues that credit card and loyalty revenue supports better lounges, seats, food and inflight connectivity. He’s largely right, and the case goes further: credit cards support more flights.

An airline becomes more attractive to cardmembers when it flies where they need to go. It also needs destinations they want to redeem their miles for. Delta has explicitly connected its growth in Austin and Raleigh with acquiring American Express card customers. A flight that looks weak based only on ticket revenue might make sense once you count the card spending it helps generate.

As I discussed in my recent piece on Scott Kirby and credit card economics, a customer might choose an airline’s card because its Chicago schedule works for their business travel, then redeem the miles for Hawaii. Assign all the card revenue to Hawaii and you can end up cutting the flights that made someone want your card in the first place.

A better seat and lounge help sell that relationship, too. And an alliance makes the card more useful by offering places to spend miles that the airline doesn’t fly to itself. Of course airlines can manage this badly. Sell more miles while planes are full, without making enough desirable award seats available, and customers wind up with growing balances they struggle to use. Sell more lounge access without adding enough capacity and the customer gets a line at the door.

The alliance has to get its members to participate in making those benefits valuable. Asked whether oneworld should set minimum protections around changes to earning, status qualification and award availability, Ott describes the programs as largely sovereign and emphasizes a spirit of cooperation. Asked how much say the alliance has over the number of award seats a member releases, he calls it a collaborative process. I’d put it a different way: an alliance trying to influence airlines is pushing on a string.

It’s the problem I’ve written about with airlines holding back their best awards from partners. They want to offer their members access to everyone else’s seats. But making their own best seats available can benefit another airline’s credit card business, while keeping those seats for their own members can help sell their own miles.

Ott makes the case that a redemption can introduce someone to an airline and turn them into a valuable customer. That’s true as far as it goes, but those seats have an opportunity cost and getting the airline with the seat to value that speculative future business enough to release it (for a foreign customer who might not travel with them often and probably won’t take their credit card) can be a challenge. So can getting the partner buying the award seat to pay enough to make that worthwhile.

Blackburn says oneworld is improving how quickly miles reach accounts following a flight across the alliance, with everyone expected on a new standard by the end of the year. He also says oneworld’s earlier artificial intelligence round the world booking assistant is gone, despite earlier claims of a fivefold increase in booking conversions.

The interview returns to the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September, where I spoke about how artificial intelligence gives customers better tools to choose rewards programs. (The summit photo below is courtesy of oneworld.)

Ott mentions verifying elite status without relying on screenshots that someone can easily manipulate. I saw a presentation at the summit for a product that was basically Plaid for airline status: the customer logged into their existing airline account to demonstrate their status to another company. I questioned whether airlines would allow that access to their systems.
