#6179. Are Mount Everest climbers dreamers, or just cultists?

In the title of his 1997 bestselling adventure tale, “Into Thin Air,” mountaineer and writer Jon Krakauer employs a double entendre so clever that its effect is extraordinary. Throughout the book, Krakauer recounts his attempt to summit Mount Everest the year earlier in what would become, at the time, the mountain’s deadliest season. I’ve been momentarily halted by that title each time I’ve picked up my tattered $5 thrift-store copy over the last few weeks. It’s witty, but not grim; accurate but also imaginative. In three words, “Into Thin Air” conveys not only the literal effect of Everest’s high altitude and how quickly the mountain can take a life, but also the ardent, almost fatuous confidence of those who choose to climb it.

The dissonance between reason and ambition is what makes “Into Thin Air” such a compelling read. For someone like myself, who knows next to nothing about climbing, Krakauer powerfully elucidates the pull of a mountain like Everest and the trance-like state in which it ensnares its adversaries. Unlike some climbers, Krakauer can wax poetic while staying honest about the stakes. He writes about mountaineering as a spiritual practice, good for the mind and body alike, while questioning why some find that clarity only by staring death in the face. In that respect, extreme climbing is an incredibly selfish endeavor. Before he begins his push for the summit, Krakauer remembers his wife, Linda, telling him before he left for Nepal: “If you get killed, it’s not just you who will pay the price. I’ll have to pay, too. For the rest of my life.”

That sentiment echoed in my mind throughout “Everest: The Other Side,” the remarkable new documentary from National Geographic, helmed by “Free Solo” and “Nyad” co-directors Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin. The film is brutally honest in its depictions of cold human narcissism and the relentless pursuit of glory in the name of nebulous spiritual fulfillment. Yet it’s just as candid about humanity’s collective desire for all those things in one form or another.

Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, “Everest: The Other Side” forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.”

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

As “Everest: The Other Side” asserts, nothing in this already mystifying life is ever so simple. The film’s subjects, mountaineer Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson, found love at the edge of the world and made a life together, with Morrison becoming co-parent to Nelson’s two young sons. But their shared lust for adventure created a prickly tension within their family unit, a strain between their passion and parentage that sits at the documentary’s emotional center.

Like those pulled by devout religion or extreme acts of faith, Morrison and Nelson are powerless before their distinct higher calling — especially with the literal highest calling of all, Everest, in their sights. They don’t just want to summit the mountain from its treacherous north face; they want to be the first people ever to ski down it. In their quest, personal glory and public vanity are forever at odds. Such a wanton, helpless display of pride makes for a character study as gripping as it is frustrating. From that disharmony, “Everest: The Other Side” forges a uniquely human story of actualization at all costs, revealing the true price of a life spent looking up and not around.

Because this is National Geographic, the film is only partially concerned with relaying that price. This documentary is made for IMAX-loving, secondhand adventure seekers. Those who want sweeping shots of impossible sights won’t be disappointed.

But while “Everest: The Other Side” includes countless breathtaking sequences of Earth’s tallest mountain and plenty of nail-biting anxiety in the eventual summit push and ski attempt, those moments are merely the film’s selling points. The crux of this story is on Nelson and Morrison’s shoulders, and their sincerity flies in the face of good judgment and self-editing, giving viewers a palpable sense of their egos. This isn’t to say that either of them is a raging narcissist who cares only about themselves, but there’s no doubt that their sport’s seismic, life-altering dangers are on full display, warts and all.

Early in the film, Nelson tries to communicate the draw of climbing, and how fundamentally at odds it is with her role as a mother. “People ask me, ‘How do you find balance?’” she says. “There isn’t. It’s just chaos. You’re just hanging on. You want to be with your family, but you have a passion, and you want to work, and you need to make money. You’re all over the map.”

It would be easy to dismiss Nelson as selfish, or, at the worst and most damning, a bad parent. How can someone have young children and decide to part with them for two months for a climb that is about, at face value, little more than bragging rights? How can a parent let their children spend two months wondering if their mother is dead or alive?

These are easy questions to ask from the comfort of a living room or the cushion of a theater seat, but much harder to answer when you’re living the life. It’s important to remember that, in life, most of us have desires that would yank us in severe directions. It reminds me that cult experts will tell you that any of us could fall into the clutches of a cult, and those of us who argue otherwise are likely among the most vulnerable. Anyone who insists they are too self-aware to be pulled into something that goes against their own interests is admitting that they don’t know themselves or humanity very well. That’s one of life’s great mysteries: Why do we do things that we know are wrong, or bad for us? Death and taxes might be certain, but so are mistakes and regret, no matter how much we’d like to believe that we’re big enough to let go.

Conflict is ever-present in Morrison, who chooses to climb Everest despite its perils. For him, the adventure is about more than pride or titles; it’s about honor and love. The journey is intended both to strengthen his bond with Nelson and honor the memory of his late wife and their two children, who died in a horrific commuter plane crash in 2011, a decade before he and Nelson decide to attempt Everest. Recalling the aftermath, Morrison tells how climbing brought him clarity. Unable to move from the edge of his driveway, consumed by grief, he eventually found the strength to simply walk up the slight incline and into his home — a microscopic example of the human spirit’s extraordinary tenacity he hopes to commemorate in the Everest climb.

We are an arrogant species, frustrated by our humble place in this ecosystem. And yet, we feel everything intensely. When we love, we want to take that love to the ends of the Earth. We want physical proof of emotions we cannot put into words. Maybe then all of this will mean something.

But more tests lie ahead. The route to Everest proves demanding in heart and health. And while training together for the big summit push by climbing a lower peak in Nepal in 2022, Nelson loses her footing in an avalanche the size of a small snow drift. On a ski slope, the drift would be minor. But on a mountain, every movement is measured. Nelson is swept away and under the snow, toward a cliff. We see it happen in real time, captured on a helmet GoPro. The moment is almost unassuming in its speed, but it permanently shapes everything that follows. Nelson is lost amid a series of avalanches, and the clock starts ticking.

Counting the seconds seems futile. But climbing is futile, too. For Morrison, left to search for his partner amid the snow, hazardous ridges and cliffs, it all seems like a waste. More pain, more trauma, more memories that are left for only one person to hold onto. I was immediately reminded of what Krakauer’s wife told him by satellite phone before he began his push from Everest’s base camp. “Saying goodbye to you was one of the saddest things I’ve ever done,” he remembers her saying. “I guess I knew on some level that you might not be coming back, and it seemed like such a waste. It seemed so f**king stupid and pointless.”

Want more from culture than just the latest trend? The Swell highlights art made to last. Sign up here

It’s hard not to dwell on that sentiment, already knowing what and who Nelson would leave behind if disaster struck. On some level, and to some people, it is all stupid and pointless. But that split second fortifies Morrison, confirming that his quest to Everest is for everyone that he’s lost, and every heartstopping moment along the way. It’s a spiritual pursuit, the kind that we make when we travel to a family member or friend’s favorite place to scatter their ashes; the kind that we make when we give eulogies, or just sit in the grass, staring into space, thinking about everything and nothing, everyone and no one.

Some may be driven to climb Everest just to say that they did it, while others are looking for something else, something with no name. They want to pierce the heavens and reach through the atmosphere to grasp the indescribable truth that unites us all. And if they don’t make it back down to share that peace with the rest of us, it might be enough to experience it just once.

#6178. Why Airbnb Is Spending Big on LA Elections

Photo Credit: Cars parked near the Hollywood sign, one of Los Angeles' most famous landmarks. Pexels / Daniel Semenov

Airbnb’s LA election spending is framed around the 2028 Olympics. A bigger bet could be on the rules after the Games.

Few companies have spent more on Los Angeles’ elections this year than Airbnb, which has put millions behind Mayor Karen Bass and other local candidates.

Airbnb’s spending touches several fights that matter to its business in the city, including a proposed temporary easing of short-term rental restrictions during the 2028 Olympics, which are expected to draw in roughly 2 million visitors to the greater Los Angeles area. As much as $4.3 billion in direct visitor spending is expected to benefit hotels, restaurants, and retailers, according to a study from the Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation commissioned by LA28.

Airbnb is looking for a bigger slice of that spending.

Since 2018, only primary residences have been allowed to list on platforms like Airbnb. Proposals for a vacation rental expansion would ease restrictions through the end of 2028.

A restriction rollback — even a temporary one — could help Airbn

Airbnb has spent more than $12 million on Los Angeles politics since 2025, backing Mayor Karen Bass, city attorney candidate John McKinney, and two City Council candidates, while pushing a Vacation Rental Ordinance that would temporarily let second homes be listed through the end of 2028. Los Angeles has limited short-term rentals to primary residences since 2018, and the 2028 Olympics — expected to draw roughly 2 million visitors and $4.3 billion in direct visitor spending, according to a study commissioned by LA28 — is the opening Airbnb is using to argue the city needs more lodging. The City Council struck the vacation rental program from the budget it adopted in May, and the planning department's August framework would sunset eased rules in December 2028, limit permits to individual owners and trusts, and cap them at about 15,000 units — a cap planning says the city has too few second homes to reach. City finance staff estimated the program might generate $25 million to $30 million in tourist tax, well below the up to $110 million cited by Airbnb's coalition. Los Angeles hoteliers, including the general manager of the Hoxton Downtown LA, told the Council the city's 113,750 county hotel rooms are already enough for the Olympics, World Cup, and Super Bowl.

#6177. The power of Latinas’ Trump regret could swing this election

This story was originally published by The 19th.

This story was originally reported by Mel Leonor Barclay of The 19th. Meet Mel and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

RIO GRANDE CITY, Texas â When Cynthia Villareal voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, she did so trusting his campaign promises of lower gas prices, border security and âassistance for the people â for the middle class.â

The 43-year-old mother of four turned out for Trump alongside a sizable majority of voters in heavily Latino Starr County, which hugs the border with Mexico and had reliably turned out for Democratic candidates for five generations.

Less than two years later, Villareal said the promise of her vote never materialized. âHe said gas prices were gonna go down. They havenât â they havenât at all,â said Villareal, who drives around the Rio Grande Valley for her job supervising home health aides and feels every little surge. Villareal manages workers in a shortstaffed, tough profession where wages have simply not kept up with the cost of living. Many of her best workers, she said, are immigrants without permanent legal status experiencing the brunt of Trumpâs immigration agenda.Â

âI mean, he didnât mention that these ICE agents were just going to be picking up all of these hardworking employees, you know, that have no backgrounds,â Villareal said, referring to immigrants without a criminal record. âTheyâre leaving people without their family, basically, and then some of the people are even dying in there,â she said of immigration detention. âLike, who knows what theyâre doing to these poor people?â

For Villareal, life is more expensive, and her job harder. âItâs just too much.âÂ

Latina votersâ rightward shift was a crucial part of Trumpâs reelection in 2024, and while more Latino men backed the president, Latinas actually made larger strides to the right in the last four presidential cycles.Â

Ahead of the midterms, Latinas are also registering higher levels of regret when thinking about their support for Trump, a dynamic that may decide the outcome of competitive races from Texas to Florida and beyond.Â

Voters like Villareal shed light on how Trump regret among this swingy and powerful group of voters âÂ Latinas vote at higher rates than Latino men â may be the swell that breaks into a blue wave for Democrats this November.Â

âI do think the narrative of this election could be that Latina women, in particular, help decide who is in control of the House of Representatives and the balance of government. And I say that because of the shifts weâve seen over time and the shifts back that we are seeing now among Latina women in particular,â said Stephanie Valencia, who studies Latino voters at Equis Research.

Latinosâ political power this cycle is spread across the midterms map. Latinos make up at least 15 percent of the population in six of the 17 most competitive congressional districts, as well as in 29 other districts considered broadly competitive, mostly in the Southwest, California and Florida. Latino voters could be the deciders in competitive races for the U.S. Senate in Texas and Florida. Also in Texas, Latinos could swing the most competitive governorâs race the state has seen in years and, in doing so, elect the first Latina to the stateâs top job.Â

Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

âTrump appealed to their pocketbooks and people were suffering here. I also think people were tired. Weâve been Democratic for over 100 years â why donât we try something different?â said Cecilia HernÃ¡ndez, who founded the local political group Somos STARR this year in response to the big swings to the right sheâs seen in her community.Â

In an interview at the office of her familyâs trash collection business, HernÃ¡ndez said votersâ views are shifting this cycle.Â

âI think along with everything thatâs happening with immigration and with the cost of living today, what Iâve been receiving a lot is, âIâm in the middle,ââ HernÃ¡ndez said. âThey donât want to be seen as far right, and they donât want to be seen as far left, either.â

Latinas stand out in just how much they are feeling the burn of rising costs. They report higher levels of financial stress and are less optimistic about the national economy, according to multiple surveys of Latino voters conducted over the past year.Â

An expansive survey of Latinos conducted in the spring and sponsored by UnidosUS, a Hispanic civil rights and advocacy organization, found that Latinas are more likely than Latino men to say that they have trouble meeting expenses â 23 percent of women vs. 17 percent of men. Men are much more likely to say they can meet their expenses and even have a little left over.

Thirty-eight percent of Latinas voted for Trump in 2024, versus half of Latino men, according to one high-quality analysis, driven by high costs and lack of confidence in the party in power on the economy. The UnidosUS survey of 3,000 Latino voters found that almost a third of Latinas who voted for Trump had regrets about their vote âÂ  seven points more than Latino men.Â

Regret is most striking among young Latinas: 42 percent said they would not vote for him again, a 12-point gap with young Latino men. Latina voters are more likely to register and turn out to vote, and with Latino voters skewing younger, young Latinas wield outsize political power.Â

âLatina women have a large gender pay gap. We also have higher unemployment. We also generally have the responsibility of going to the supermarket and paying the grocery bills and understanding that eggs and and everything else is more expensive,â said Katharine Pichardo, the president and CEO of the Latino Victory Project, which backs progressive Democrats. Latinas are more likely to be closely involved in their kidsâ education and doctorsâ appointments, a frontline view on rising costs that Pichardo said shaped how they voted in 2024 and their views on that vote now.Â

Melissa Morales, the president of Somos Votantes, which does political outreach to Latinos on behalf of Democratic candidates, said Latinas started peeling away from Trump almost immediately in his second term, while Latino men started shifting in the latter part of 2025.Â

While Latinos, like voters overall, broadly rank the cost of living as their top issue, the disparate impact of the administrationâs immigration policies on Latino communities is also registering among Latino voters.Â

A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid October found that only a third of Hispanic voters approve of the administrationâs handling of immigration. UnidosUSâ survey found significant gender gaps between Latino men and women. While both groups rank the importance of the issue about the same, Latinas were more likely to oppose policies like ending birthright citizenship and more funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Latinas were also more likely to support banning ICE from sensitive locations like schools and hospitals and to support requiring warrants for enforcement at home or in a workplace.Â

Some of the most dramatic shifts toward Trump and Republicans in 2024 were logged in Texasâ Rio Grande Valley, where Villareal lives. A string of counties in this part of Texas saw double-digit shifts in Trumpâs favor compared with the 2020 election, after significant shifts to the right from 2016 to 2020.Â

Latina voters in the Rio Grande Valley and around Texas will have a big impact on the Texas governorâs race, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa is locked in a dead heat with three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Hinojosa describes herself as a populist who will tackle corruption and undue influence in government, which she ties to rising costs, weakened public schools and more.Â

Hinojosa rarely acknowledges the history-making potential of her campaign as a Latina in a state that has never elected a Latino to the governorâs mansion. She instead nods to it by saying that sheâd be the first governor from the Rio Grande Valley, which for Texans may as well mean the same thing.Â

Hinojosa, who is bilingual, flexes her Spanglish easily on the stump, telling voters that the most important lesson she ever got came from her mother was the scolding, âNo te dejes.â It doesnât have a direct translation in English.Â

âThe best thing I can come up with is, âKnow your worth and defend it,ââ Hinojosa said in an interview. Asked if the Spanish phrase was connecting with voters, Hinojosa said, âfor sure with Latinos, and 1,000 percent with Latinas.âÂ

âIâve learned on the campaign trail that this is a saying that is mostly passed down through the women in the family,â she added. âAnd I think itâs because of this knowledge that women have for their daughters, grandmothers have for their granddaughters, that the world is tough, and we have to be strong.âÂ

At campaign events in the Rio Grande Valley in September, several voters cited Hinojosaâs identity and approach to politics as a motivating factor.Â

Juanita Vallejo, 40, of Edinburg, Texas, said she sees Hinojosa as an âempowered woman,â and likes her firm stances in support of public schools and curtailing data centers.Â

âI donât want to say it this way, but Iâm going to say it â she wouldnât kiss ass to Trump. I think she would stand up to what is right,â said Rosie Hernandez, 56 of McAllen.Â

Hinojosa is one of the breakout candidates of the cycle, but she has had to plead for funding from national Democrats hesitant to spend in Texas. Earlier this month, a group of influential Latinos in Democratic political circles put pressure on Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association (DGA), to invest $10 million in the Texas governorâs race. The DGA decided to send $1 million.

Valencia, who signed onto the letter, said Democratsâ investment in Hinojosaâs race has larger implications for the party and sends a message to Latinos. âSheâs a once-in-a-generation candidate from a state that is disproportionately Latino that has been the unicorn that Democrats have chased for decades,â Valencia said.Â

âTo have such a young, dynamic, charismatic Latina candidate in this environment and to not back her is a statement in and of itself, and it says a lot about how certain national Democrats feel about Texas and how they feel about certain candidates.âÂ

Hinojosaâs ability to build enthusiasm for her campaign after starting out with a low profile as a state legislator from Austin could bode well for one the biggest challenges when it comes to Latino voters: turning them out.Â

Latinos had the lowest turnout rates among the major racial and ethnic groups at 51 percent, compared with 71 percent among White voters and 60 percent among Black voters. Nearly 6 million eligible Latinas did not vote in 2024.

During a town hall in Houston with a local Latino influencer this month, Hinojosa mused about the event likely being the first time a candidate for governor hosts an event in Spanish. Before Hinojosa arrived on stage, the host ushered to the microphone a woman who identified herself as a 46-year-old Houston native who had never voted before. Holding a white and orange slip, she said she had registered to vote earlier that day. âQuiero cambio,â she said to cheers. âNo more Trump.âÂ

As both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential election, theyâll have to contend with the fact that the Latino vote is a swing vote. Whatever gains Democrats make this cycle, they have a lot of ground to make up â especially with Latinas.

Nine days out from Election Day, Villareal said she is planning to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot. She described her vote this time as against Republicans â a register of regret â rather than about enthusiasm for the Democrats on the ticket.Â

âWe have to trust somebody. We have to vote for somebody no matter what,â Villareal said.Â

âAnd obviously, the way things went in 2024 with Republicans, there wasnât a change at all. Itâs just been worse. So weâre gonna try and see.â

A lot of these stylish, boutique hotels enter the points world through curated hotel collections that participate in loyalty programs, giving hotels a wider reach of potential guests without having to adhere to strict brand standards that change the spirit of the property.

One of the pioneers in this space is Design Hotels, a collection of hundreds of independently-owned hotels and resorts dotting the globe, each with its own identity, personality and approach to hospitality.

"Every hotel is picked for its originality [and] the vision that's behind it," Stijn Oyen, managing director at Design Hotels, told TPG, adding that each property has "a strong point of view and cultural connection."

And it's not necessarily easy to make the cut for this collection: According to Oyen, only about 5% of the hotels that apply to join Design Hotels are accepted in an effort to "stay true to the original roots and values of what makes a design hotel."

Then there's the loyalty twist: Marriott actually owns Design Hotels, and many (but not all) of the collection's properties participate in Marriott Bonvoy.

Here's a quick guide to everything you need to know about Design Hotels, plus a few standout properties where you can earn and burn Marriott Bonvoy points.

Related: 12 new boutique hotels worth redeeming your points for

Founded in the early 1990s, Design Hotels was created to bring together independently owned, design-forward hotels that shared a commitment to originality, creativity and local culture.

Today, that collection is more than 300 members strong, with new properties regularly joining. What differentiates the collection is the individuality of each property — each one has its own unique point of view, rather than a prescribed set of standards travelers will see at more traditional hotel brands.

"We're set up around design," Oyen explained. "It's about the vision. It's about being independent with a voice."

Design Hotels became part of Marriott's portfolio following the hotel giant's acquisition of Starwood Hotels & Resorts in 2016, giving Marriott a majority stake in the company. By 2021, Marriott had acquired full ownership of Design Hotels, though the collection continues to operate as a separate entity, with member hotels retaining their individual identities and independence.

The company describes its properties as "design-driven hotels that function as social hubs and spaces for purposeful experiences."

But what does that actually mean? To start, getting into the collection isn't easy, and Design Hotels is looking for one distinguishing factor before choosing a new member: "the originality in its concept."

According to Oyen, only about 5% of applicants pass the test. Hotels are also evaluated on everything from design and sustainability to cultural programming and the property's connection to its local community.

"It's a strong, strong sense of place," Oyen explained, adding that beyond their physical design, the hotels should have vibrant public spaces that attract locals and feel like an extension of the neighborhoods they call home.

It's also about the people. According to Oyen, about 60% of Design Hotels owners are first-time hoteliers, bringing fresh perspectives and new approaches to hospitality. The company calls the creative minds behind its properties "Originals," describing them as "the engines behind pioneering design and revolutionary hospitality," according to the brand's website.

Without rigid brand standards dictating every detail, these hoteliers have the freedom to pursue projects that seasoned hospitality pros might consider too risky. That might be as simple as removing TVs from guest rooms or as dramatic as building a hotel accessible only by cable car, like Vigilius Mountain Resort in Italy's Dolomites.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, Design Hotels offers a truly independent, boutique-like stay while still allowing them to earn and burn points. Something that, frankly, a lot of people don't realize is available to them in the loyalty world.

Just don't forget: Not all Design Hotels participate in Marriott Bonvoy. To see a full list of the 120-plus participating hotels, visit Marriott's dedicated Design Hotels landing page.

For Design Hotels, according to Oyen, the relationship with Marriott is a win-win situation: Hotels gain access to nearly 300 million loyalty members while maintaining their "complete independence."

But because these properties operate differently from traditional Marriott hotels, Bonvoy elite members shouldn't expect all their usual perks to apply.

Here's what members can expect based on their status.

The following Marriott Bonvoy benefits are excluded at Design Hotels:

Set near the beach in Casablanca, Villa Sahrai pays respect to "Casablanca’s Art Deco tradition" across its 56 rooms and public spaces. Be sure to take advantage of the spa and its Moroccan hammam before settling down for food at one of two restaurants or a nightcap at the bar.

How to book: Cash rates from around $160 per night or 34,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

To get to Vigilius Mountain Resort, guests must ascend a private cable car that travels between the mountain hotel and the village it soars above. But once up at the top, guests are treated to beautiful Dolomite views, architecture that incorporates nature and wellness experiences around every stylish corner.

How to book: Cash rates from about $341 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

At The Austin Proper Hotel, patterns, textures and colors combine in unexpected and beautiful ways from the moment guests step inside until their head hits the pillow. The hotel is as cool as Austin itself, but also full of surprises: You can grab classic Tex-Mex to eat or opt for a French Japanese tasting menu or soak up the sun at the rooftop pool before a lymphatic drain at the Verbena Spa.

How to book: Cash rates from $350 or 54,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

Kyoto is no stranger to incredible hotels, but Genji Kyoto offers an intimate experience with just 20 rooms that feel distinctly Japanese and totally sleek and fresh. As serene as they come, spend a day getting lost in Kyoto's ancient history before heading to the rooftop bar and garden to unwind.

How to book: Cash rates from about $227 per night or 47,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

Condesa is one of Mexico City's trendiest neighborhoods, so it only makes sense to stay in a hotel that also fits the description. At this hotel, enjoy rooftop sushi or French-Mexican fusion food; relax in the hydrotherapy pool or kick back on the patio and watch the city's cosmopolitan set roam the area.

How to book: Cash rates from $339 per night or 42,000 Marriott Bonvoy points.

As major hotel companies continue to expand their portfolios beyond traditional hotels, from independent boutique properties to outdoor-focused experiences, collections like Design Hotels are helping diversify what travelers can experience with points and miles.

For Marriott Bonvoy members, that means more opportunities to stay somewhere truly unique without giving up the ability to earn and redeem points. And while the elite benefits might look a little different, the chance to experience a hotel with its own distinct personality might just be worth the trade-off.

âAt the end of the day, people know who I am, they know what I stand for. Iâve consistently been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress, and ultimately, I think people will judge me based on my record and who I am,â Lawler said in a brief interview in Nanuet on Sunday, adding that people in the district âdonât actually knowâ or care who Jeffries is.Â

âI think that everybody needs to understand that if women arenât at the table, things are going to keep happening like that,â she told The 19th.Â Â Â

The pattern across the tracker is capital flowing to M&A, refinancing, and returns rather than to demand generation or distribution.

#6167. Right-wing media and the mystery of Texas’ transgender mailers

On Thursday night, the smear at the heart of the mysterious transgender mailers that have rocked the final weeks of the midterm elections in Texas completed its journey. What began as baseless social media whispers quickly ascended the ladder of conservative influence, jumped into mailboxes across the Lone Star State and ultimately into the comforting prime-time embrace of Fox News.

At a town hall in Fort Worth, a Texas mother of six named Rebekah Smith told Vice President JD Vance that her 11-year-old daughter had received a letter explaining how to transition without her parents ever knowing, and asked how Republicans would keep the government out of her family. “I don’t know who sent that letter to your child,” the vice president said, “but I think the person who sends a letter to an 11-year-old about gender transition, what I call that in my family is a pervert, and that person ought to go to prison.” Host Jesse Watters, never one to let a grievance go to waste, promised that Fox would investigate “this perverted letter.” Vance asked Smith to talk to his staff because he would “like the Department of Justice to investigate that” as well.

Watters rushed to promote the spectacle. “WHOA! Texas MOM tells JD Vance her DAUGHTER received a letter telling her TO TRANSITION TO A BOY,” he posted on X, followed by Vance’s promise. Missing from that framing was the question that should have governed the segment: Who actually sent the material?

Nobody on that stage mentioned that the pamphlet was a fake. Nobody mentioned that the real transgender advocacy group named inside it had disavowed the mailer. Nobody mentioned that sworn testimony filed that same week had tied the text messages that accompanied it to a national Republican organization. The vice president was asking federal prosecutors to chase a forgery that may well have originated in his own party’s orbit — and he was doing it on a network whose viewers had been marinating in that forgery for weeks.

The race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico has become a crucible for dark-money maneuvers. As polls show the Republican grip on the Lone Star State slipping, conservative campaigns and their surrogates have resorted to increasingly desperate tactics. In early October, for example, Talarico took a brief hiatus from the campaign trail to recover from a severe case of the flu. Rather than accepting a routine human illness, the right-wing echo chamber treated a temporary absence as evidence of mental illness. Within days, the fabricated scandal has collapsed — yet the machinery of right-wing media simply pivoted to amplifying a more insidious operation designed to trigger visceral outrage.

This second October surprise involved millions of unsolicited text messages and a wave of physical mailers sent to Texas households with materials that directed readers to the website of the Transgender Education Network of

It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward.

Texas while inserting provocative advice on child emancipation that the real organization says it never authored or authorized. By flooding the electorate with extreme material disguised as progressive advocacy, right-wing operatives appear to have sought to create a fake controversy that could be weaponized in attack ads and campaign speeches. Vance, for instance, told the Fox News audience that Talarico has “a weird fascination with trans kids,” and that “he’ll probably defend the right of the person sending the letter, not the right of the parent who is rightfully creeped out by this.” Vance claimed that Talarico “has actually called it abusive when parents try to prevent their children from transitioning” and that Paxton “has fought hard to prosecute those people, whereas James Talarico has fought hard to protect those people.” Even the distortion had been laundered by then — Talarico called denying a child’s gender identity abusive, a different claim from saying parents must permit medical transition, but at the top of the ladder the difference no longer exists.

That is how a smear works in the closed ecosystem of the American right. It does not need to survive scrutiny. It just needs to circulate upward. An anonymous account posts it; an influencer adopts it; a donor-funded outlet reports the influencer’s outrage as news; an elected official demands an investigation, and the demand becomes proof the story matters; cable news books the controversy; a vice president promises federal action. Each rung launders the one below it. The correction, when it comes, travels in the opposite direction and arrives nowhere.

The paper trail looks like what you would expect from a covert operation. Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed in Wyoming on Sept. 2 through a commercial registered agent that helps owners stay anonymous. After CBS News Texas visited the agent’s address in Sheridan, Wyoming, the agent announced it was resigning. The mailers listed a Houston-area post office box. The Texas Observer reported that the barcode on the envelopes traced to a mail-tracking company that has taken federal campaign money from only one group this year, the National Republican Congressional Committee. The committee said it had nothing to do with the mailers, and the company would not say who paid. CBS News Texas reported that the bulk-mail permit belongs to an Illinois printer owned by the Zerrusen family, who have given heavily to Republican PACs and been photographed with Donald Trump.

When the real Transgender Education Network of Texas filed a petition in Travis County court to unmask the perpetrators behind the impersonation campaign, the partisan safety nets of the Texas judiciary eventually snapped into action. A deposition of Infobip, the messaging company that delivered the texts, which a Travis County judge ordered made public, indicated that the texts were sent on behalf of the Republican Women’s Caucus Fund and a man named John Braun. But on Friday, the Texas Supreme Court, composed entirely of judges appointed by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, issued an administrative stay that blocked its release. Chris Hilton, an attorney who previously served under Paxton, defended him during his impeachment trial and was later pushed out of office amid sexual harassment allegations, argued on behalf of the company that the mailers were not political speech because they named no candidate or party.

Dirty tricks are an old tradition of American politics. This cycle, Republican PACs in Nevada mailed a flyer calling a nonpartisan candidate, Danielle Ford, the “AOC of Nevada,” hoping voters would mistake her for the actual Democratic nominee, Aaron Ford. This week also brought word that the group that funded Cornel West’s 2024 ballot drives raised every dollar through a dark-money network bankrolled by Elon Musk.

The president’s party whines about decoy candidates in Alaska while running them at home. Ratf**king is a long and proud Republican tradition, and the Texas operation fits inside perfectly.

On the surface, the electoral arithmetic in Israel appears straightforward. Parties opposed to Netanyahuâs far-right government won 67 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israelâs parliament. So a majority coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces is clearly achievable, right? You would think so, except that 19 of those 67 seats were won by Israelâs âArab parties,â an all-time high, and that startling fact has thrown the entire political system into confusion.

Netanyahu and his allies have spent the last week airing groundless allegations that the election was fraudulent or rigged, a refrain that Americans are likely to hear a great deal in coming days. What the Zionist far right means is that too many Israeli Arabs â meaning the Palestinian population that remained in Israel after the state was created in 1948 â decided to vote this time, an outcome that no one expected, and that none of the parties representing the Jewish majority particularly wanted.Â

Now, in a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.Â

In a masterstroke of historical or perhaps biblical irony, Israelâs Arab minority â which is not a monolithic group in political or cultural terms, and until now has never been electorally significant â holds the balance of power, and perhaps the nationâs future, in its hands.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former general who leads the centrist-Zionist opposition to Netanyahu, promised during the campaign not to form a government with Arab support. Over the last several nights, thousands of demonstrators in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem have urged him to do precisely that, since the only realistic alternative is the grim default setting of Israeli politics: another wobbly right-wing government headed by Netanyahu, which means more brutality and destruction in Gaza, more war with Iran and more settler violence in the West Bank.Â

As Gideon Levy of the left-leaning Israeli newspaper Haaretz explains it,Â

The future of Israel now depends on its Arab citizens and on the attitude of its Jewish citizens toward its Arab ones. Eighty years after the Nakba and the establishment of the Jewish state, Israeli Palestinians may determine its fate. Is there greater historical justice than that?

The electionâs unexpected results are âa cause for rejoicing,â Levy writes, in that they have presented Israelis with a clear choice âbetween a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu and a government that includes the Arab parties.â If the âchange blocâ within the Zionist majority cannot accept a coalition with Arab Israelis, he continues, âthey will make it clear that they are actually the same as Netanyahu, that they prefer even the devil Netanyahu over repressing their racism. â¦ [E]veryone will know that racism is the supreme value in this country, across the board, above any other value.â

That ferocious language certainly does not represent mainstream Israeli opinion, but itâs fair to say the strong emotion beneath Levyâs words is far more widely felt. I donât think itâs possible for a non-Jewish observer (such as myself), however well educated or sympathetic, to understand the anguish felt by Jewish people â wherever they live, and whatever their political views â at the enormous distance between what Israel originally represented to the world, or claimed to represent, and what it represents now.

Iâm old enough to remember when most American liberals and progressives viewed the state of Israel in overwhelmingly positive terms, as a locus of charismatic or heroic renewal for the people Hitler couldnât kill, infused with the spirit of European socialism and, not far below the surface, the collective guilt of the Holocaust. I grew up in one of the most left-liberal corners of America, surrounded by educated adults who supported the civil rights movement, opposed the Vietnam War, hated Richard Nixon and loved Israel. Golda Meir and Moshe Dayan were beloved celebrities; the Six-Day War of 1967 and the Yom Kippur War of 1973, as narrated by U.S. media, were straight-up battles between the forces of light and darkness.Â

That says more about the moral blindness or willful innocence of American liberalism, I must admit, than it says about Israel. In any event, when I saw Joe Bidenâs fateful bear hug with Netanyahu on the tarmac of Ben Gurion Airport in the aftermath of the dreadful Oct. 7 attack, I understood it. I recognized the country Biden was coming from, because I came from there too: It was the Democratic majority of the not-so-distant past, when Israel was embraced as a light to the nations and left-wing radicals who brought up the Palestinian cause were being unreasonable hotheads, if not openly antisemitic and a little bit Nazi.Â

What Israel has become during Netanyahuâs long and destructive reign is now clear to most of the world, and most of all to the many Jewish or Israeli critics who have been speaking difficult truths for many years, often at enormous personal cost. I am disinclined, however, to judge too harshly those who cling to the vision of Israel as an exceptional nation â one that has stumbled, perhaps, but may yet regain its true path.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only by Amanda Marcotte, also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Like I said earlier, we should mind the plank in our own eye first. Isnât that the same vision that many Americans still cling to? That somehow, on the other side of this dreadful phase of our history â yes, a full decade of Donald Trump, but Iâm afraid the damage goes back a lot further than that â the âindispensable nationâ variously articulated by Abraham Lincoln, John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama is still there, still retrievable, still bending its moral arc toward justice.

Americans and Israelis are conjoined by history, for better or worse, and now see each other as distorted reflections, through a glass darkly, as the King James Bible puts it. We face versions of the same decisions this week, about whose votes count and whether the highfalutin words of our constitution apply to everyone. About whether to see terror and tyranny for what they are, and turn the page.

from Andrew OâHehir on our bewildering world

#6145. The Security Challenges Facing the Next Israeli Leader

Analysis: The Security Challenges Facing the Next Israeli Leader

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.

In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.

In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

These conflicts, however, have brought with them additional problems for Israel that its new government must address. In particular, Israel has failed to translate military success into lasting strategic gains.

The Iran war is the most pressing security challenge. What was intended as a short war is now in its ninth month, with no end in sight—and indeed escalation seems possible. Although the United States is focused on the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz and the security of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and other Gulf allies, Israel is more concerned about Iran’s long-range missile arsenal and provision of drones and money to anti-Israel proxies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing the group to rearm.

More broadly, Israel must break the cycle of endless conflict. In the last three years, Israel has used military force in eight countries and territories: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Qatar, Syria, the West Bank, and Yemen. Israel’s enemies, however, show no sign of folding, even as the populations they claim to represent suffer tremendously. Israel can degrade its enemies’ military capabilities, but it is far harder to stop them from rebuilding or get them to abandon their hostility. Iran may emerge from the war wounded but vengeful, and it may commit at least some of the resources it gains under any cease-fire agreement, such as the one the United States proposed in June, to countering Israel. Hamas and Hezbollah are far weaker, but Hamas is still the most important Palestinian actor in Gaza, and Hezbollah, too, remains formidable.

This lack of progress makes Israel’s wars unsustainable even as their human cost is staggering. In Lebanon, Iran, and the West Bank, Israeli operations have killed thousands of civilians as well as many enemy fighters, while the civilian figure for Gaza is in the tens of thousands. Israel has devastated infrastructure in Gaza and parts of Lebanon, with mass displacement in both areas. Even if the new Israeli government places little weight on this suffering, other countries do, and support for Israel is low in most of the world.

Israeli leaders may dismiss this general collapse in support as a necessary price to pay for its security, but it also shapes how key allies treat the country. Israel has long hoped to secure an alliance with Saudi Arabia, but this is politically impossible for Riyadh when the deaths of Palestinian children are a regular feature in the news.

Pollster Dahlia Scheindlin on whether Benjamin Netanyahu can stay in power.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Early results indicate deadlock in parliamentary elections.

Far more consequential are the effects on Israel’s relationship with the United States. Polling by the Pew Research Center indicates that only 16 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans have favorable views of the Israeli government. Among young adults, those figures are 12 percent for Democrats and only 28 percent for Republicans.

The United States supports Israel militarily, economically, and diplomatically, as well as being a partner in the Iran war. Even if most forms of support continue, the coming years could see increased congressional scrutiny of military assistance to Israel, less diplomatic support in the United Nations and elsewhere, and a possible decline in financial support.

Because the endless wars draw on Israeli reservists, they are also increasing strains in Israeli society. In addition to the risk of casualties, the reservists are away from their jobs and families for long stretches, with no end in sight. There is an Israeli joke that one-third of Israelis pay taxes, one-third work, and one-third serve in the military. The joke is that it is the same third, as Israel’s large Arab population and most of its ultra-Orthodox community do not serve. Reflecting this disproportionate burden, one contentious issue in the latest election was the question of whether Israel’s large and growing Haredi population should be forced to serve in the military.

Historically, Israel has excelled at operations and tactics while having a short-term, narrow mindset about how to achieve security in general. As one Israeli security official joked to me on a recent trip, “The Hebrew word for ‘strategy’ is ‘tactics.’” This mentality has helped Israel score impressive military victories over Hezbollah and Hamas, but it has also left Israel trapped in multiple endless wars with little hope of lasting security. The new Israeli government, whether led by Netanyahu, Eisenkot, or another figure, must translate military dominance into sustainable political arrangements. Otherwise, Israeli society risks exhaustion while the country loses vital international support.

Daniel Byman is a professor in the School of Foreign Service at Georgetown University and the director of the Warfare and Irregular Threats Program of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. His latest book is Spreading Hate: The Global Rise of White Supremacist Terrorism. X: @dbyman

#6141. The strange new math behind the price of your groceries

Walmart recently published a list of things it promises not to do to its customers.

âWe price the product, not the person,â Walmart CEO John Furner announced in a September letter to customers. âYour income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay wonât change the price,â he promised. Nor, he said, would the retailerâs AI shopping assistant, Sparky, use information customers shared to raise prices or conceal cheaper options.

This was nice to hear. I hadnât previously considered that telling a computer I needed toilet paper might result in an emergency toilet-paper rate. There is something faintly unnerving about the specificity of a corporate reassurance, particularly when it introduces several possibilities you hadnât thought to worry about.

It made me preemptively nostalgic for the little paper price tag beneath a box of cereal. Thereâs something reassuringly stupid about it. It tells you what the cereal costs. It doesnât know how much money you make, whether youâre in a hurry or what the temperature is outside. Unless an employee comes along with a new sticker, the person reaching for the same box ten minutes later sees the same number. A modest achievement, perhaps, but one Iâm growing increasingly fond of.

The appeal isnât really the paper. Itâs the transparency of the arrangement. As retailers gather more information about their customers and acquire increasingly sophisticated pricing tools, shoppers risk knowing less about why theyâre paying what theyâre paying. The problem isnât simply higher grocery bills. Itâs the possibility of a transaction in which one side can examine the other in exquisite detail, while the other can barely see the rules.

What prompted the letter from Furner is that Walmart is expanding its use of electronic shelf labels, little screens that let employees update prices digitally from a central computer instead of replacing stickers by hand. The change makes sense. Furner points out that updating paper tags is tedious work, and heâd rather employees spend their afternoons helping customers than tending to a small forest of adhesive rectangles. Digital labels can also help ensure the price on the shelf matches the price at checkout.

And electronic labels arenât, in themselves, surge pricing. Walmart says it doesnât use them to change prices according to who is shopping or the time of day. But efficiency is a different question from trust. Making a price easier to change isnât necessarily a problem. Making it harder to understand how that price was reached might be.

Want more great food writing and recipes? Sign up for Salonâs free food newsletter, The Bite.

Weâve already accepted a surprisingly elaborate set of conditions for saving money on groceries. Download the app. Make an account. Remember the password. Clip the digital coupon before you leave home. After handing over our personal information and completing several minor administrative tasks, weâre permitted to save 75 cents on yogurt. The store, meanwhile, gets a rather detailed account of our preferences. What happens when that bargain runs in reverse?

Last December, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found that shoppers using Instacart were sometimes shown different prices for identical groceries from the same store at the same time. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., an 18-ounce box of Signature SELECT Corn Flakes appeared for $2.99, $3.49 and $3.69, depending on whose screen you were looking at.Â

Instacart said the shoppers were assigned to pricing experiments randomly, not sorted by income, demographics or browsing history. It ended the tests after the investigation. That distinction matters, especially because the research didnât establish that anyoneâs personal habits were being used against them. But it demonstrated how quietly prices can diverge when the shopper sees only the number assigned to her. You canât question a difference you have no way of seeing.

I buy a lot of black beans. Enough, presumably, that a supermarketâs software could identify me as a woman with firm opinions about legumes. If that earns me a coupon, wonderful. Iâm considerably less enthusiastic about the possibility of an algorithm deciding that my apparent dependence on black beans means I could stand to pay another 30 cents per can. Itâs one thing to recognize a loyal customer. Itâs another to recognize a captive audience.

Other pricing algorithms raise different questions (McDonaldâs, for instance, faces a lawsuit alleging AI-assisted price coordination among franchises, which the company denies). Prices have always fluctuated; coupons have always rewarded some shoppers more than others. Nor should computers be banished from the business of deciding what things cost. But the supermarket is not an airline, and dinner should not require the same vigilance as booking a flight.

Walmartâs promise is worth taking seriously. The company has drawn a clear line around how it says it will use customer information, and thatâs preferable to leaving shoppers guessing. But itâs a corporate commitment, not a rule every retailer must follow. And the fact that a supermarket now feels obliged to assure us it wonât charge extra because we seem hurried or financially comfortable suggests how strange our expectations have become.

Perhaps itâs naive to want a supermarket not to use what it knows about me against me. Still, I donât need the price tag to know me. I need it to tell me what the cereal costs.

#6138. Why Trump’s Hail Mary on Fuel Prices Fell Short

Analysis: Why Trump’s Hail Mary on Fuel Prices Fell Short

Understanding the conflict four years on.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s eleventh-hour pivot back toward Moscow in a desperate bid to lower fuel prices ahead of next week’s midterm elections is not going great. But neither is his war on Iran, with oil prices climbing toward $120 a barrel and one U.S. lawmaker describing the administration’s plans for a renewed war on Iran as “insane.”

Three weeks ago, in a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump made a deal to purchase Russian diesel, which is forbidden under U.S. law. While the measure would have involved risible amounts of additional barrels into a strained global market, it has descended into farce. The three Russian tankers loaded with fuel may not be allowed to dock in U.S. ports. U.S. energy traders are unwilling to chance running afoul of long-standing sanctions against buying Russian energy. And Democratic lawmakers have said that any buyers will face congressional and legal scrutiny.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s eleventh-hour pivot back toward Moscow in a desperate bid to lower fuel prices ahead of next week’s midterm elections is not going great. But neither is his war on Iran, with oil prices climbing toward $120 a barrel and one U.S. lawmaker describing the administration’s plans for a renewed war on Iran as “insane.”

Three weeks ago, in a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump made a deal to purchase Russian diesel, which is forbidden under U.S. law. While the measure would have involved risible amounts of additional barrels into a strained global market, it has descended into farce. The three Russian tankers loaded with fuel may not be allowed to dock in U.S. ports. U.S. energy traders are unwilling to chance running afoul of long-standing sanctions against buying Russian energy. And Democratic lawmakers have said that any buyers will face congressional and legal scrutiny.

The global benchmark price of oil, which was about $70 a barrel before Trump started the Iran war in February, rose to over $117 a barrel on Friday. U.S. nationwide average gasoline prices are $4.20 a gallon, more than a dollar higher than the year before; no president ever has kept gasoline above $4 more than Trump. Diesel, which powers the entire economy, is worse: At $6.32 a gallon, it is about 70 percent higher than one year ago.

Another of Trump’s pro-Russia moves to keep energy prices in check was a pressure campaign on Kyiv to refrain from targeting Russian oil refineries with drones and missiles. U.S. negotiators including Steve Witkoff said that Kyiv should show “gratitude” toward Washington by curtailing strikes.

Ukraine complied for a spell in October, before remembering that what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calls “long-range sanctions” are the country’s best way of severing the sinews of Russia’s war machine. Overnight Thursday, Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil targets, with a devastating attack on a large Rosneft refinery that makes jet fuel for the military.

U.S. leverage over Ukraine is less than it used to be, since the Trump administration has not delivered any new military or financial assistance since Trump took office for a second time, and on several occasions, including this past month, has suspended what assistance there is, including some access to Starlink’s military-grade satellite internet service and intelligence sharing about inbound missile strikes. (While Ukraine has pleaded in vain for additional missile interceptors, the United States has pleaded poverty. This week, the United States sent a Patriot air defense system from Texas to Israel ahead of an anticipated restart to the fighting in the region.)

The U.S. pivot to Russia isn’t limited to diesel deals and strong-arming Ukraine, though. In addition to stopping future aid, U.S. officials have reportedly been cautioning countries on the front line of Russia’s shadow war to tone down their warnings about Moscow’s hostile intentions. And on Friday, the U.S. welcomed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to the G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, to the irritation of European allies. The abandonment of Ukraine has lately raised bristles in the European Parliament, where some politicians are redoubling their support for Ukraine even as Trump retreats.

“This is not one of those instances of many different shades of gray. There’s clearly an aggressor who is in the wrong, and that’s Russia, and so I think, for me, that stands clearly,” said Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European Parliament from the Volt Europa party and a vocal critic of Russia’s invasion.

Kyiv’s energy war on Russia may hurt on the margins, but the real culprit is Trump’s war on Iran.

It won’t help consumers, won’t help Kyiv, and won’t mean riches for Moscow.

But Trump’s travails aren’t limited to his limited leverage over Ukraine. The war in Iran, which is now in its eighth month and likely to escalate in coming weeks, has kept oil prices high as shippers struggle to navigate a strait strewn with high costs, Iranian drones and missiles, and, for the first time, limpet mines.

It may get uglier after the midterms. The Trump administration is reportedly considering a sharp military attack to try to once and for all break the back of a regime that has withstood war and sanctions for nearly half a century. Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, who was briefed on defense planning, described the war plan as “insane.”

None of Trump’s moves to placate Putin will help him in the midterms, but they could haunt him in the two years remaining in his presidential term. Winter is coming for Ukrainians who endure daily and undefended assaults from Russian missiles, but it may be coming as well for an administration that has aided and abetted.

#6137. Fox News loses its grip on the culture wars

In any other election cycle, a viral Fox News gaffe would have registered only as a momentary laugh. Last week, reporter Lucas Tomlinson was covering a South Carolina rally for incumbent Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who is seeking to serve a full term following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. In reality, the event was more about Donald Trump, who had flown to the Palmetto State to help shore up Grahamâs candidacy, which increasingly appears to be at-risk. Spotting a middle-aged white man with a beard, Tomlinson assumed he was about to get some choice footage of a gushing Trump superfan. Instead, Tom Hoyle, with an admirable deadpan, joked that he had turned out for the rally because he was too young to have witnessed the 1978 Jonestown massacre, in which 918 followers of Rev. Jim Jones died after drinking a fruit drink laced with poison. âThereâsÂ nothing like seeing a cult right up front, man,â he added.

âAll right, maybe this is not a Trump supporter,â Tomlinson said, scurrying away.Â

The surreal moment capped what has been a desultory midterm election season for Fox, a network that bills itself as ânewsâ but has long been seen by fans and detractors alike as Republican propaganda. Despite their largely worshipful coverage of the president, Trump has been complaining that the network isnât doing enough to salvage the campaigns of the GOP.Â

âFoxNews is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates,â he recently posted on Truth Social, echoing his prior complaints that the network focuses too much on the Democrats running this cycle than on their Republican opponents.Â

Trump is not wrong about the coverage tilt. According to Media Matters, during this election cycle the network has mentioned the names of Democratic candidates at over three times the rate of Republicans. That disparity, though, doesnât mean the coverage is sympathetic. To the contrary: Fox producers likely recognize that this yearâs GOP field of candidates is deeply uninspiring. Some, such as Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor of Ohio, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is seeking a Senate seat,Â are so repulsive that even lifelong Republicans canât pretend to like them.

This season, Democratic candidates are making more compelling TV, particularly the charismatic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Michiganâs Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Texas state representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton. The most Fox News can hope for is to hijack these candidatesâ ability to command attention, and then use it to drive negative polarization with endless âwho do these people think they are?â outrage. But then again, the network knows its audience.Â

As Salonâs Sophia Tesfaye recently noted, itâs not like Fox News knows what else to do. The hosts, she writes, have been grabbing wildly at straws, praying they can find any story to spark culture war hysteria that will distract voters from serious issues like inflation, the war with Iran or the metastasizing deportation crisis. The network tried to make hay out of the French riots, but even Fox viewers struggled to see why student protests in Paris matter to America. It attempted to pretend Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., was calling for mass arrests of young Republicans when she was asked during a recent appearance about holding the GOP accountable, but that never really caught on either. A last-minute gambit to feign outrage over Barack Obamaâs recent joke comparing Trumpâs White House decor to the Cheesecake Factory fizzled out as well, likely because it simply reminded people of how the current resident is defiling the Peopleâs House.Â

Part of Foxâs problem is immediate. Many votersâ economic woes are sky-high, making it hard for culture war nonsense to feel relevant. But thereâs also a longer-term problem for the network, which is that they donât make as much sense as they used to.

Fox News has long existed to dress up gutter bigotries and far-right paranoia in the clothes of respectable news coverage, mostly through the use of dog whistles and innuendo. In the past, winks at some of the fouler ideas out there was enough to titillate the audience while keeping up the pretense of respectability. But now, that stuff seems dated and out of touch.Â

This is an era when, as Jamelle Bouie of New York Times said on YouTube, the actual president offers âKlansman-level racismâ from the campaign stump, calling Black people âlow IQ,â flinging a slur for transgender people at Democratic politicians and suggesting that El-Sayedâs Muslim faith makes him a terrorist. Right-wing social media, especially the Elon Musk-owned X, reads like Stormfront message boards from the 1990s, with Musk himself regularly promoting white nationalist ideas and memes. Former Fox hosts Megyn Kelly and Tucker Carlson offer their former employer stiff competition by being more dishonest and outrageous than the lawsuit-wary network can be, with segments suggesting only supermodel-hot women get raped or that Holocaust deniers have a point.Â

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

But according to Salonâs Alex Galbraith, one Fox host seems to be getting sick of his networkâs culture war strategy. Jesse Watters has complained openly on air about how bad the GOP is doing and how Fox coverage isnât doing much to excite their audience. In one particularly telling segment, he lashed out about the relentless attention Fox News gives to non-stories from the WNBA, including hysteria over trans players, of which there are zero.

âI donât want to push this story anymore!â Watters said. âI want to leave this story alone! I am no longer talking about the WNBA. As of now, I boycott this segment.â

Although his reasoning may differ, the host is right that the Fox fixation on the WNBA is stupid. The league has become such an obsession on the right because, plainly put, many male conservatives hate seeing female athletes perform feats they couldnât even manage in their youth. They want to end professional womenâs sports and return to the sexist delusion that all men are stronger and faster than all women. This much is evident in how real-life right-wingers behave toward the WNBA, such as going so far as to buy tickets so they can throw sex toys at the players.Â

Fox hosts are careful to never say outright that women shouldnât play sports; that, as they well know, could alienate millions of Republican voters, especially women and fathers of female athletes who are more moderate on this issue. Instead, the network attempts to hijack the antipathy many conservatives feel toward female basketball players with their traditional wink-and-nudge coverage, pretending they want to âclean upâ the sport. This preserves the illusion that the right doesnât hate female athletes while portraying the players â the white ones at least â as fragile, helping to reassure an insecure male audience.Â

In the past, this kind of tap dance has worked. Now, as Watters implied, itâs floundering, feeling much too tepid when compared Foxâs online competitors and actual politicians flinging unprintable slurs. Watters suggested as much during another segment, when he argued that Republicans need more âfear pornâ if they want to win.

His use of the word âpornâ is telling. Watters was arguing that it doesnât do to be coy any longer â that only the hard-core stuff will move the base. But for Fox News, that would come at the cost of losing advertising dollars and the eyeballs of less radical viewers. This is a true dilemma â and itâs one that couldnât happen to a more deserving network.Â
