#6132. Ali Velshi is on the Big Board now

Six years ago, Donald Trump dropped â11th Hourâ host Ali Velshiâs name at several campaign rallies as an example of the so-called âfake news mediaâ getting what the president thought he deserved: a taste of âlaw and order.â

In May 2020, while covering the Minneapolis protests that arose in response to the murder of George Floyd, MSNBCâs live coverage caught Velshi being struck in the knee by one of the rubber bullets police fired into the crowd.

Months later, Trump referred to the incident multiple times on the campaign trail as âthe most beautiful thing,â earning laughter and applause from supporters. But an emotional Velshi recalled that moment differently in June 2026, as he said goodbye to his old weekend showâs audience.

In that moment and others, he told âVelshiâ viewers that democracy, fairness, transparency and accountability took yet another hit. âThis is how it unfolds. Not always with legislation, not always with imprisonment. Sometimes with a rubber bullet. Sometimes with a police escort. Philosophy repeated until enough people believe it. . . and they believe that the next step becomes possible,â he said. âThe press is not the enemy of the people. The press is the peopleâs guarantee that they will know what is done in their name.â

Then, he reminded everyone watching that the midterm elections were 148 days away.

When I spoke with him last Thursday, the veteran journalist repeated his belief in the pressâ witnessing role, unshaken by the massive changes occurring in the news industry.Â  One of those changes places him at the networkâs famous Big Board as the chief data reporter for MS NOWâformerly MSNBCâcarrying on an election-night tradition made famous by Steve Kornacki.

Velshiâs on-air analysis will be augmented by an additional feed called VelshiCast, a behind-the-scenes look that will stream on MS NOWâs YouTube channel.

Other aspects of MS NOWâs live coverage remain familiar to longtime MSNBC viewers, with Rachel Maddow leading the channelâs supergroup of Nicolle Wallace, Chris Hayes, Jen Psaki, Lawrence OâDonnell, Stephanie Ruhle, Michael Steele, Symone Sanders Townsend, Ari Melber and Peter Alexander.

As for Kornacki, he became NBC Newsâ chief data analyst after NBCUniversalâs owner, Comcast, spun off MS NOW along with USA Network, Syfy, E!, and its other cable channels into a venture known as Versant.

Journalism is in a precarious time, but this administration has placed particular pressure on TV newsrooms. With Paramount Skydanceâs acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, CNNâs and CBSâ teams are facing rounds of buyouts and return-to-office orders to thin their ranks. Meanwhile, Status reported that October 2026 is Fox Newsâ lowest-rated month since December 2023, with the network averaging 1.1 million total-day viewers.

Velshi remains optimistic about his profession, as he said in our wide-ranging conversation about his plans to make the Big Board even more essential on this midterm election night.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Salon: A lot of coverage cited what you said in your farewell message for your last weekend show. One of them, and I think this is important, is that you were reminding people that the show was ending 148 days before the midterm elections.

Well, weâre here now. Youâve started your weekday show, and Iâm curious to hear your impressions of how you think things are going, in terms of that dialogue with viewers and whatâs coming up about Tuesday from a data perspective.

Thanks for actually thinking that through because there is a real through line. I miss my old show a lot, but you know, that moment was so important. What I was trying to do that night, and what Iâve been trying to do since, is convey the idea that this isnât about partisan politics. This is about civic engagement. This is about democracy, and nobodyâs going to do that for you, right? Democracy is not something you pick off a shelf. It is work for all of us all the time, and I donât think weâll ever be free of a moment when democracy is on autopilot.

And so, right now, everybodyâs responsibility is to participate actively. I have a sense that pretty much all of our regular viewers, certainly people in our MS NOW community, are heavily engaged. Theyâre big consumers of news and information. They probably already voted. If not, theyâre planning to, because some people just like voting on election day because itâs exciting. But this moment wants more of us. It needs us not just to vote, but to be engaged in the dialogue, to commit to democracy, to help other people vote, to feel like we are in community with each other, to save democracy.

This doesnât matter whether youâre a Democrat or Republican or an independent, or you donât even think politics matters to you. And I will say that since that day that I left the show, Iâve only felt stronger about this, and Iâve only felt that people are understanding their assignment very, very well. And weâre seeing this from a data perspective.

Every single day, we get new data that shows early voting and advance voting. It is remarkable. At the low end, the states are up 20% compared to the last midterm elections in 2022. Weâre not even bothering to compare it to a presidential election because theyâre different beasts. In some states, early voting is up 40%. Now, what would possibly explain that? Itâs enthusiasm amongst voters. So people are going out and theyâre taking the assignment very, very seriously. Iâm very heartened by that.

So letâs talk about your new role and what you do with the data, and the conversation you have with people about that. Because I think that especially around elections, some of our pessimism and optimism comes from polling, but not necessarily from data.

Youâre 100% right. Thank you for that question too. I led the show on Monday night with three people: Kabir Khanna, whoâs our head of data and analytics; Dave Wasserman from the Cook Political Report; and Larry Sabato from the University of Virginiaâs Crystal Ball. These are the three data nerdiest guys around.

I think itâs important to understand that raw data is of no use to anyone. Even slightly interpreted data is of no use to anyone. You have to be able to look at it holistically. You have to look at polls and also understand their margins of error. You have to understand trends in polling so that even if a poll is good, meaning itâs statistically sound, that doesnât mean itâs correct. Polls have errors, and then the decision about how an election goes depends in part on polling, in part on trends, in part on the weather, in part on the news cycle, in part on whether your decision in an election is because youâre voting in favor of someone youâre excited about or youâre voting against someone youâre mad at.

I think raw data without analysis should be a crime â¦ OK, in this world where people make crimes out of everything, Iâm not sure thatâs the right thing to say. But my point is, itâs really bad. Itâs bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope that they interpret it. Itâs also bad for democracy to throw raw data at people and hope they follow it. Like, what am I trying to tell you? If I tell you these races are all ahead, I may not be giving you useful information for you.

So part of it is also managing expectations amongst voters. A âblue waveâ or a âbig blue wave,â I donât use that terminology . . .Â  But Iâll give you a range. Iâll tell you that as of today, the Democrats are likely to win a minimum of eight seats in the House and a maximum of probably in the mid-30s. Thatâs probably the range. Might I be wrong? Absolutely. But thatâs what I want people to understand. And then Iâm going to give you the clues to understand how I got there, so that you can follow along with me. Iâd rather make a data interpreter out of everybody who watches us than be their data interpreter.

â[P]eople are understanding their assignment very, very well.â

In terms of the election night and you being at the BigÂ  â are you guys still calling it the Big Board?

We are. Yes. I tried to call it The Magic Board of Wisdom, but no one took to that.

What you and Kornacki were doing at the Big Board really became a thing over the last decade or so.

People learned to consume election night coverage based around it. I know a lot of folks who may not necessarily watch every single moment of coverage, but keep an eye on developments with the sound off, based on whatâs going on with the Big Board. Itâs kind of like a lot of folks might go into a restaurant or a bar with the TV tuned to a game, but on mute. Iâd like to know how you feel about that mode of consumption.

Well, look: The bottom line is, scientifically, peopleâs visual consumption is their No. 1 source of information consumption. I mean, you can make the argument that smell is actually more important for your survival, but weâre not talking about survival here. The visual component hits before the auditory component does, so thatâs never going to change.

What may change is whether people watch it on their phone or their TV or, you know, through AI glasses, but the visual component is still stronger for everyone than anything else. So we spend a lot of time adjusting the size of the boxes on TV and deciding whether there are too many of them, and whether this is helpful information or confusing information. We want to make it very obvious that this is complicated information, and weâre working hard because itâs our job to present this to you in a way that is consumable and accessible. Which, by the way, has been sort of my stock in trade for my entire career.

So Iâm committed to making this the most visually easy experience. If you donât have audio, and if youâre sitting in a bar or sitting on a plane or wherever, and you canât hear me, youâll still understand everything thatâs going on.

In this election, thereâs emotional sentiment, psychological underpinnings, and consumer sentiment to account for. How much are you able to go into those factors on election night? Because each is also locally dependent. We have a lot of reporting determining the key races, but if you look down the ballot beyond the candidates, you have initiatives and other legislation driven by sentiment.

So we have two ways of measuring sentiment. One is in what we call our voter poll. Thatâs what you would know of as an exit poll, right? We do that in partnership with others. Itâs probably 1000 questions that really allow you to put meat on the bones of the result you just saw.

And I actually think thatâs one of the sad things about fast-moving election coverage, is that you sometimes donât get to sit there and say, âLet me explain to you. We actually know. We asked these voters why they made the decision they made, and they actually told us. So we donât have to extrapolate. We donât have to, you know, twist ourselves into pretzels. We actually have that information.â

âOur capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.â

So I will tell you, a lot of that will happen prior to polls closing. So people think to themselves, âYour coverage always starts before the polls close, or before the polls close in the place that I care aboutâ â thatâs actually where you get the most context. So weâre going to start early in the evening on Tuesday with our exit polls. I think we release them at 5 oâclock, and thatâs great information.

And then subsequently, we are covering every one of those ballot measures. In fact, thatâs part of what Iâm studying today. Iâm studying both the exit polls and the ballot measures today to really understand how theyâre going to correlate with the results.

You know, Iâm an economics reporter, so things like consumer sentiment are really, really clear to me. You know, people keep saying the economy is the most important thing in this election. I remind people the economy is the most important thing in pretty much every single election there is, with the exception of an actual war in which Americans have troops on the ground or an international threat. Thatâs the truth. People care most about how this affects them.

I think thereâs an interesting intersection in this election between people who care about the things that affect them, like the economy, gas, things like that, and people who care about democracy deeply. The second one can be a bit of an extra abstraction for people. The first oneâs absolutely not. So I have to measure how I tell those stories.

So Iâm going to take a little bit of a 30,000-foot view here and look at this in terms of MS NOWâs position in the news industry. On one side, you have Fox, part of a massive media conglomerate, with ratings declining right now, days before the election.

And on the other, CNN. Thereâs a lot of restructuring going on there related to the Skydance merger, a lot of conversation about that. And then thereâs you guys. Iâm wondering if, at this point, things feel different, just in terms of what youâre able to do.Â  I donât necessarily mean just kind of financial resources, but also what kind of backing Versant is giving you this time versus when you were part of the larger NBC Universal structure.Â  I realize this is still a very new situation, but again â Iâm curious about the pros and cons.

At the moment, itâs all pros. So first of all, weâre the scrappy, leaner player in the game now. . . Can we compete with other people? Yes, we can, and weâre doing it very well. As I said, the things that matter â the ability to conduct the analysis, and I donât mean that just for the big board â weâre able to do that. We are going to match everybodyâs expertise and probably exceed it.Â  Our capabilities are better today than they were a year ago.

No. 2, weâre literally the tip of the spear for the conversation that is happening in America right now around what country do we want to be. How is this solvable? Weâre right there.

And Iâm sorry for the folks around us who are dealing with these structural issues and trying to figure out what they are and how to represent themselves in this moment of turmoil, but weâre not struggling with this at all.

But we are not one thing, right? We are covering the story with all the complexity of an electorate that is spread out along the political spectrum. Iâm sure there are some of our viewers who love the idea that the [Democratic Socialists of America] is ascendant, and there are some of our viewers who love the fact that there are ex-conservatives, ex-Republicans like David Jolly running for governor in Florida. Or that there are some Republicans who are running for office because theyâve demonstrated their ability to be independent thinkers. We have the ability at MS NOW to have those discussions across the political spectrum. Weâre very comfortable with it.

In 2024, I interviewed Lawrence OâDonnell right before the election, and we talked a lot about the state of journalism, and specifically how effective the media was in terms of questioning Trump and holding him accountable. I think weâve seen shifts since then, but Iâd love to know whether youâve seen any shift one way or another.

I think so. Once in a while, maybe even daily, Iâll see some headline from a mainstream news organization that makes me cringe. That makes me think: Are these reporters and editors not understanding the moment that weâre in? Are they not understanding that that weirdly neutral headline that you just wrote doesnât actually communicate what just happened? It doesnât capture the fact that your reader and your viewer and your listener are shocked and possibly outraged and really struggling with whatâs going on. But you just wrote a headline that looks like this is just a governmental development, something that the Department of Justice did.

I think most of us are better at this than we were in 2024, and certainly better than we were in 2020 and 2016. Yes, weâve all gotten a lot better. There are still remnants in mainstream media of journalists who treat the activities of this government and this administration as normal, and thatâs not a journalistically difficult thing to unwind, right? Itâs not.

Itâs not difficult to say that journalism exists for two reasons: to bear witness for those of our consumers who cannot bear witness on their own because they canât travel to go see the scene, they canât go to the protest and they canât go to the press conference. We are there to bear witness, and we are there to hold power to account. Thatâs it. If you are not doing those two things every single day, you are not doing your job.

And there are still some members of the mainstream media who are not doing their job. This has nothing to do with what your opinion is or where you are in the political spectrum. Are you bearing witness and are you holding power to account? I think we are generally better at that. Now, what that has done is result in lawsuits. It has resulted in bans for some of us from the White House. Thatâs the consequence of doing your job properly, and thatâs okay. We will meet and face the consequences. Weâll fight back, and we will fight for our right and our viewersâ and our listenersâ and our readersâ rights to get the information that they deserve. Thatâs how you can tell weâre doing a better job at this. When they come for you, it means youâre doing your job.

#6128. What in the World?

Quiz: What in the World?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

1. How did right-wing presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro react to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s runoff election victory on Sunday?

He called for his followers to protest his loss in Brasília.

He said he would request an annulment of the election.

Lula became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in history to come from behind to win the election’s second round, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports. Bolsonaro, the subject of several criminal probes, subsequently fled to Miami, where he called himself “the leader of Brazil.”

2. Student-led protests in Serbia that began in November 2024 culminated in the defeat of longtime right-wing leader Aleksandar Vucic in elections on Sunday. What incident sparked the original demonstrations?

Vucic’s decision to send military equipment to Russia

The collapse of a concrete railway station canopy

A factory spill that polluted the Danube through Belgrade

The revelation of a mass domestic surveillance network

The student protesters’ improbable victory against the Vucic regime could be instructive for their counterparts in the United States and European Union, Edward P. Joseph writes.

3. The Chinese Communist Party’s fifth plenum began on Monday. Traditionally focused on economic policy, what is the priority for this year’s gathering?

The shift in focus is a sign that Chinese President Xi Jinping is worried that his anti-corruption campaigns aren’t paying off, FP’s James Palmer writes in China Brief.

4. Early results show no clear winner from Israel’s parliamentary elections on Tuesday. But what is clear is that voter turnout was at its highest this century. About what percent of Israel’s registered voters turned out to cast a ballot on Tuesday?

Even if the opposition bloc succeeds in forming a governing coalition, there is little indication that Israel’s policies toward Palestinians will dramatically change, FP columnist Steven A. Cook writes.

5. At a Texas rally on Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump floated adding a 51st state. What territory or country did he suggest?

Trump’s “America First” foreign-policy agenda has been wildly unpopular with voters, as recent polling indicates, Jonathan Monten, Jordan Tama, and Josh Busby write.

6. The third Russia-Africa Summit began on Wednesday in Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin asserted that Moscow would champion greater African involvement where?

In the continent’s own critical minerals industry

At the World Bank and International Monetary Fund

African leaders’ attendance has dipped since its high point in 2019, partially driven by Moscow’s unfulfilled promises on the continent and the forced recruitment of Africans into Russia’s military ranks to fight in Ukraine, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

7. Why were three French nationals sentenced to life in prison in Iraq on Thursday?

For spray-painting protest graffiti on Iraq’s parliament building

For smuggling weapons to the Popular Mobilization Forces

The arrests highlight how conflicts and divisions that may feel distant to Washington remain alive and pressing in the Middle East. Earlier this month, Hekmat Aboukhater wrote about how the Trump administration is inflaming sectarian divisions in Iraq.

8. Ireland said on Friday that it will set up a government body that, for the first time, would research and prepare for the possibility of what?

Sending troops to defend Palestinians in the West Bank

Unifying with the U.K.-run Northern Ireland

The announcement comes as Scotland and Wales also push for greater autonomy from London, which has reeled from years of dysfunction, Jamie Maxwell wrote in May.

9. Contestants gathered in Belgium on Monday to participate in a competition to see who could craft the most impressive sculpture made from what material?

Among the chocolate creations were birds, an elf, and a praying mantis, as photographed by The Associated Press.

10. An Australian court ruled on Monday against an inmate’s claim that his inability to have this product violated his right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.” What product did the inmate sue to access?

The court found the ban on Vegemite, a yeast-based spread, was justified because of the product’s potential to impair drug-sniffing dogs’ ability to detect narcotics as well as its possible use in brewing alcohol, The Associated Press reports.

#6121. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6120. ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’

Analysis: ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

As Election Day approaches, the president of the United States is onstage, lambasting the powerful forces ranged against him—the judges, the media, the ultra-wealthy. Addressing 20,000 of the millions of regular Americans who love him, he defies his enemies, declaring, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred!” The crowd roars.

Oct. 31 marks 90 years since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt delivered that speech at Madison Square Garden, as the 1936 presidential race neared its climax. In a world again beset by angry populists stoking economic distress, the rise of autocrats, and the floundering of moderate politicians, Roosevelt’s barnburner speech has come to seem relevant once more.

As Election Day approaches, the president of the United States is onstage, lambasting the powerful forces ranged against him—the judges, the media, the ultra-wealthy. Addressing 20,000 of the millions of regular Americans who love him, he defies his enemies, declaring, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred!” The crowd roars.

Oct. 31 marks 90 years since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt delivered that speech at Madison Square Garden, as the 1936 presidential race neared its climax. In a world again beset by angry populists stoking economic distress, the rise of autocrats, and the floundering of moderate politicians, Roosevelt’s barnburner speech has come to seem relevant once more.

Roosevelt had entered office ready to work with established power as he launched his reflationary, state-expanding New Deal. Yet the president had grown increasingly frustrated by the obstructiveness of the Supreme Court—which had blocked programs such as the National Recovery Administration, designed to end “cut-throat” competition—and by the hostility of newspapers and tycoons. His enemies insinuated that he was a communist, and a would-be dictator. He also faced the rise of the radical right, which sought to exploit the public’s fear and frustration.

Roosevelt realized that by facing down the “economic royalists,” as he put it in his acceptance speech at the 1936 Democratic National Convention, he could cast himself as the people’s tribune, uniting the disparate groups supporting him. In that speech on Halloween, he warned that “powerful influences” were striving to bring back leaders who were “indifferent” to ordinary Americans’ economic plight. “Government by organized money,” he charged, was “just as dangerous as government by organized mob.” He hoped in his second term to become such forces’ “master.” Three days later, almost 61 percent of voters backed him, in one of the most decisive presidential election victories in U.S. history.

The speech resonates today even in that land of actual royalists, the United Kingdom. In the 2019 general election, the left-wing Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn quoted Roosevelt’s speech. But since then, political commentators, most of whom were never keen on Corbynism, have done the same. Their overarching goal is to ensure, as Roosevelt did, that power does not fall to the radical right.

In 2024, Corbyn’s successor, Keir Starmer, lead Labour to back into office, in an election marked by widespread public frustration with the long-dominant parties. From the left, the Greens and “Gaza independents” made gains, while support for the far-right party Reform UK hit 14 per cent—and has continued to rise. When it became clear that the new prime minister’s response was to remain stolidly managerial while at times adopting the language of Reform’s own arguments, liberal-left fears rose too.

In the two years that followed, a series of voices—in the Guardian, the London Times, and elsewhere—called for Starmer to learn from Roosevelt’s tub-thumping at Madison Square Garden. The prime minister, they argued, should pick battles with entrenched interests, carving out a clear narrative about how overcoming those interests would improve voters’ lives.

Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn speaks at Birmingham City University in Birmingham, England, on Nov. 21, 2019.Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

Writing in Prospect magazine, Ben Ansell, professor of comparative democratic institutions at Oxford, was one of those arguing that the speech offered the center-left a model for beating the radical right by using its own populist means against it. In January, as Starmer’s popular support plumbed terminal new depths, the veteran pollster Peter Kellner called on him to learn from Roosevelt’s speech by “declaring war” on the champions of Brexit. “Would he be taking a risk?” Kellner added. “Absolutely — and that’s the point.”

Starmer didn’t have it in him, but this was never just about his personal skillset. Across the democratic world, the center-left has been under pressure for a decade to find effective ways to respond to right-wing populism, as exacerbated by social media. Now that Starmer has been replaced by the former mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham (a politician much more ready to talk about power), those same voices reiterate their case. They point to the punchier approach taken by the prime ministers of Spain and Australia, and the success of Manuela Schwesig, the Social Democratic premier of the east German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in holding back the advance of the extreme right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

Political scientist Robert Ford is the author of books on the radical right and Brexit. He plays his students at the University of Manchester footage of Roosevelt’s speech, he told me, because “it shows us how much bolder a center-left politician was 90 years ago.” As the center-right loses ground to its more populist rivals, he argued, the left and the radical right are “coalescing around in-group/out-group politics at a mass level, whatever politicians do.” This is forcing center-left politicians to ask themselves, “How can we best make use of this?” Roosevelt’s us-against-them speech offers a useful example, Ford suggested, because the genial president delivered “a polarizing message in a non-polarizing tone”—a trick he thinks Burnham is well-placed to copy.

Read More In this black-and-white photo, Teddy Roosevelt points to the middle of South America on a map as another man looks at the map from the other side of it. Both men wear suits, ties, and wire-frame glasses. In this black-and-white photo, Teddy Roosevelt points to the middle of South America on a map as another man looks at the map from the other side of it. Both men wear suits, ties, and wire-frame glasses. The ‘Donroe Doctrine’ Is a Roosevelt Redux Then as now, big stick diplomacy will lead to costly cycles of intervention and retrenchment. Argument | Tom Long, Carsten-Andreas Schulz

Then as now, big stick diplomacy will lead to costly cycles of intervention and retrenchment.

Within weeks of Starmer’s election, the Guardian columnist and historian Andy Beckett exhorted him to emulate Roosevelt’s speech. Now, nearly two and a half years later, Beckett told me that the more consensual tone struck so effectively by social democrats in the buoyant 1990s has been “tested to destruction.” In a period of widespread economic insecurity and visibly extreme inequality, “if social democracy has any chance now, as in the 1930s, it’s got to be much more aggressive rhetorically.” Roosevelt’s example, he said, offers a way for center-left leaders to unite with their more left-wing colleagues against a common enemy.

Each of those pointing back to the speech appears to have alighted on it independently, as they combed history for ways out of the British center-left’s constraints. This makes it all the more striking that they all homed in on the same oration, and a U.S. one at that. But then, Britain’s political pantheon lacks a figure like Roosevelt: at once centrist by instinct, radical by necessity, and charismatic by nature. Perhaps the nearest equivalent is Tony Blair, but he was never driven to declare war on entrenched power in the midst of economic crisis.

The question Roosevelt’s example raises for today’s Labour leaders is: which enemy? Ansell said that Burnham tried targeting the bond markets, which “didn’t work quite so brilliantly.” He might focus more fruitfully on exploitative gambling companies, Ansell suggested, or right-wing British tycoons who denounce their home country from tax exile. Or the heads of the United Kingdom’s notoriously inefficient privatized utility companies.

Ford, however, contends that Labour should concentrate its fire on perhaps the most aggressive expression of private power: big tech, and specifically Elon Musk. As populists have demonstrated, putting a face on the enemy can help dramatize political fights, and bolster public support. In the wake of a series of inflammatory interventions over such issues as immigration and free speech, Musk is very unpopular in the U.K. In 2025, he appeared by video link at an extreme right rally in London and told the crowd that “you either fight back or you die.” A few months later there came the scandal over Musk’s AI, Grok, producing images of child sexual abuse. Ford suggests Musk’s public stances make him “a golden opportunity for any center-left populist looking to do a bit of an FDR.”

Roosevelt signs the Glass-Steagall banking reform act at the White House in Washington on June 16, 1933.Universal Images Group/Getty Images

In the United States itself, where the radical right is already in power, Roosevelt’s speech has been pressed into service too—but not by the sort of moderates from whom critics long to hear it. In 2018, Maureen Dowd of the New York Times used it to criticize Barack Obama for failing to take an Roosevelt-style approach to the bankers who caused the 2008 crash. While this was historically unfair—Roosevelt, like Obama, initially bailed the banks out—it highlights the fact that Roosevelt’s controversial address remains the province of those to Obama’s left.

Elizabeth Warren has embraced the speech since at least 2015; Bernie Sanders has repeatedly conjured it too, as in a speech on June 13, 2019, where it triggered a raucous standing ovation. In 2025, Jamie Raskin clipped the speech in a tweet endorsing the “Rooseveltian” now-Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani.

In April, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar used it to help launch the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ 10-plank agenda for this year’s mid-term elections, which is focused on stopping “price gouging” by corporations and “[abolishing the unlimited spending power of Super PACs.” Much more contentiously, the far-left streamer Hasan Piker used the line on X to fend off accusations of antisemitism, after saying that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action.”

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders delivers a speech in Washington, D.C., on July 17, 2019. Cheriss May/Getty Images

Casar’s approach seems much more effective than Piker’s, explicitly aiming to bring left and moderate Democrats together around economic policies intended to re-channel populist anger away from the targets that President Donald Trump attacks, toward those the left blames for the cost-of-living crisis. For this to work, however, moderate Democrats might need to go beyond their attacks on “billionaires” and “the Epstein class,” and strive to match the bravura of their most successful ancestor.

The real lesson of the speech is not that welcoming the hatred of plutocrats is always effective, no matter who says it. Those lines landed precisely because they were not delivered by an angry leftist, but a cool-tempered centrist, driven finally to declare that the vested interests had gone too far.

In the United States, as in the U.K. and elsewhere, the potential impact of adopting Roosevelt’s strategy lies in that clarifying surprise.

Phil Tinline is a documentarian and journalist and the author of Ghosts of Iron Mountain: The Hoax of the Century, Its Enduring Impact, and What It Reveals About America.

#6116. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trumpâs trusted lawyerÂ and cable newsâs favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Boratâs ultimate get in 2006âs âBorat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,â the pranking of Americaâs mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: hisÂ corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to succeed in theirÂ mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohenâs exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.Â By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout âSubsequent Movefilmâ for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment weâre introduced to Bakalovaâs Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on parÂ with the sinking of the Titanic.Â Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, âthe happiest wife in the world,â emboldening her to join Boratâs latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Boratâs government, have not been kind to him since âCultural Learningsâ conquered America with great success â high five! â 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstanâs current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, heâs hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form â ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all â and given a new mission to smooth glorious leaderâs entry into the worldâs strongman club. How? By presenting toâVice Premier Mikhail Penceâ valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, âKazakhstanâs Minister of Culture and No.1Â porno star.â

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the filmâs release fails to ruin âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas, Â plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the filmâs full title: âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series âWho Is America?â â which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American â enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit heâd pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. âTheyâre fun!â

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, âSubsequent Moviefilmâ makes Tutarâs empowerment the centerpiece of the movieâs second half. Â Baron Cohenâs signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Wolinerâs past TV work (which includesÂ series such as âNathan for Youâ) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

Thereâs the practical matter that the character ofÂ Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that âthe problem with success, although itâs fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I âgetâ with Borat again, so itâs a kind of self-defeating form, really.â

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today.Â However, heâs right about the problem of Boratâs fame. âSubsequent Moviefilmâ confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Boratâs relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant â except for when he revealshis subjectsâ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original âBoratâ donât involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Boratâs stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in âSubsequent Moviefilm.â Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctorâs office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohenâs infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama âwith the Wuhan flu.â

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business donât tell us anything we donât already know. Instead, itâs what the context implies about Americaâs psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isnât merely in the pastorâs misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutarâs stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutarâs father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesnât disturb the status quo.

Thereâs the Texas baker who uses icing toÂ pipe the wordsÂ âJews Will Not Replace Usâ on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. Thereâs theÂ shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the âno means yesâ dress section. Thereâs the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, âWhat color is best for racist family?â says without pause or reaction, âI wouldnât go any darker than a six or a seven.â

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; sheâs also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first âBoratâ and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, sheâs a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of âSubsequent Moviefilmâ relative to the first âBoratâ sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has arenât deadly, although itâs plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the filmâs ending in ways that donât feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the âBoratâ of 2006 and the 2020 âSubsequent Moviefilmâ is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trumpâs election in 2016, to say nothing of howÂ decline and fall of basic critical thoughtÂ has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, thereâs simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If thereâs a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called âlesserâ nations.

Now it doesnât allow the audience to be so sure of itself,Â implying in the final sceneÂ that we arenât merely ugly Americans. Weâre a once glorious nationÂ being led by goons who areÂ sliding us backwardÂ into diminishment, and dangerously so. ThatÂ is nothing to laugh about.Â

âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6113. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

#6112. Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Review: Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

Chances are you know about the original Stanford prison experiment. In August 1971, with the campus on break, a psychology professor at Stanford University named Philip Zimbardo offered a paying gig to students willing to run through an unusual and morally questionable exercise. The basement of a university building was made up to resemble a prison. Twenty-four students (all male, all white except for one Asian-American; “good boys,” Zimbardo called them) were randomly split into groups of inmates or guards and given appropriate uniforms. For two weeks, the professor thought, he would take notes on how unchecked power in an enclosed system would reveal itself. The experiment, funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research, ended after six days, and that’s only because Zimbardo’s girlfriend stopped by and said, “Holy crap, what the hell is happening here?!”

Stanford professor Philip Zimbardo discusses the Stanford prison experiment on Aug. 20, 1971.Duke Downey/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images

At least that’s the lore. Zimbardo—a wonderful self-promoter later taken to wearing t-shirts with the letter Z resembling Superman’s logo—seemed eager not just to lean into his experiment’s findings, but to allow that he, too, lost his ethical mooring, suggesting that all closed institutions are incubators of depersonalization and madness.

You can watch this all play out in a pretty good fictionalized version of the experiment produced in 2015 called The Stanford Prison Experiment, adapted from Zimbardo’s 2007 book The Lucifer Experiment. In it, Billy Crudup plays Zimbardo, Michael Angarano plays a guard nicknamed John Wayne, and Ezra Miller and Tye Sheridan play the inmates who suffered the most, eventually quitting.

Indeed, the fact that the experiment went haywire and needed to be canceled surely aided in spreading its premise—that merely donning the costume of guard or inmate in a sealed-off environment would radically alter someone’s personality, and rather quickly. These findings, plus the inherent “wait, they let students do this?” question, made Zimbardo a notable and sought-after voice on cable news during the Abu Ghraib scandal.

But recent research and a three-part 2024 documentary that aired on the National Geographic channel, The Stanford Prison Experiment: Unlocking the Truth, offers firsthand testimony from the participants that they were coaxed to behave in ways that would conform to the experiment’s thesis. John Wayne, for example, wasn’t really a skull-cracking bully as the film clips suggest, but a pot-smoking theater kid who wanted to please his director. One of the kids who quit wasn’t on the verge of psychological collapse; he just thought the experiment was annoying and was told the only way to get out of it was to pretend he was losing it.

All these decades later, it’s hard to know which version is accurate. (As with so much in life, it is likely somewhere in between.) But the suspicion surrounding Zimbardo’s data is, I suppose, reason enough to call for a redo.

The punchline, of course, is that however bogus the original may actually be, this new iteration is a hundred times more manufactured.

Trymaine Lee and host Alison Wood Brooks in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

Enter television producers Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth, whose previous work includes competition shows like Project Runway, Top Chef, Nailed It!, and my personal favorite, the ongoing Is it Cake? franchise, which has somehow managed to stretch the act of wondering whether something is cake for three seasons plus five holiday-themed specials. With that eternal question still lingering, they decided it was time to turn their reality TV lens to issues of crime and punishment. (One wonders how Rodion Raskolnikov’s life would have been different had he had access to fondant.)

“Does power corrupt?” is the big question laid out in the first of six episodes in The New Stanford Prison Experiment. Our host—the Ryan Seacrest of this affair—is Alison Wood Brooks, an associate professor of business administration at Harvard University and a behavioral scientist, and she assures us this experiment will answer this question once and for all. Her two associates offering color commentary are Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer-winning journalist and author, and Michael Cantrell, a retired federal corrections officer and podcaster.

In a decommissioned wing of an actual county correctional facility in Georgia, the trio sit before a bank of monitors from their panopticon’s perch, which naturally includes a whiteboard featuring circled names, flowchart markings, and vague phrases like “test ourselves.” They observe the activity of the show’s willing participants as though they were Harry Lime on a Ferris wheel, strikingly detached from humanity.

And who are the participants? Unlike Zimbardo’s crew—kids looking for a summer gig—these are adults with a full understanding of what they are doing. If there is a financial incentive, it is never mentioned. What is mentioned is that everyone involved considers this is a test of their character, and that the experiment may lead to an important conclusion. What’s more, the show has intentionally kept the pool of applicants diverse in age, race, and class—CEOs and bartenders walk side by side in their civilian clothes before the selection begins.

Contestants wait to join the experiment in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

The original experiment left who would be an inmate versus a guard completely up to chance. Not so here. The producers have predetermined this, but the audience isn’t privy to how they made their decisions. (The three women are guards because someone must have wisely realized that mixing genders in a locked-down 24-hour quasi-jail was something no insurance company would cover.)

But there’s an elephant in the room. Unpleasant though this may be, no one is actually incarcerated or in anything resembling danger. There are cameras everywhere, and all anyone needs to do is say the safe word (“pineapple”) and they are free to go.

Also, all of the inmates have clearly been encouraged to give periodic first-person addresses (cleverly shot through glass to resemble a visiting room)—a very common reality show trope to add narration and assist in the editing process. Annoyingly, while watching the finished product, we have no idea how scripted these moments are, or when during production they were recorded. Also, everyone, from all walks of life, uses Instagram-friendly therapy speak phrases. Great for marketing clips.

This is the perfect project for the creator of ‘Adolescence.’

Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus” asks whether an AI-led society would really be that bad.

Over time, some personalities begin to shine. One of the younger inmates, Pete, who has a Jesse Eisenberg-like quality, is a fifth-grade social studies teacher who feels compelled to instigate and push back against authority. His reasoning is hazy, but he seems to be working toward some poorly defined, somewhat utopian ideal. (The show works mostly in soundbites, not thorough arguments.) He quickly finds some teammates in the art of pushing back, one specifically who seems even more eager to be a thorn in the guards’ side, even though Pete is quietly calling the shots.

The guards, meanwhile, are split into a night and day shift, and an alpha male soon finds himself the unelected leader of each. On night shift, there is Chris, an entrepreneur with a coaching business and an intense desire to be liked. He enforces rules but does it with a smile. On the day shift, there’s Chet, a supervisor on an oil rig, who seems more than eager to carry the metaphorical big stick.

The guards get printed memos (not unlike directives from the Gamemakers in The Hunger Games) with certain tasks and directives. They are to vote for a head guard among them on their shifts (in one case reversing what seemed like natural selection) then each shift must elect what is effectively a shop steward from among the inmates. As the choices are made, our three observers titter and murmur in fascination.

Things move along largely as expected. There is discord. Much of this is due, so the experts conclude, from too much individuality, which is anathema in a prison. Chris and Chet have different styles, and this imbalance causes a rupture. When penalties (such as removing a common clock) aren’t enforced, it creates a mess.

On the seventh day of the show, longer than the original experiment ever went, there comes a new twist. Some of the guards and inmates are directed to trade places. Wouldn’t you know it, the troublemakers are now wearing the badges. How will this change things?

Naturally, the show milks this reversal for as much drama as possible, but it is ultimately quite anticlimactic. This isn’t a real prison, it isn’t even a rogue college experiment from the early 1970s; it’s a Netflix reality show. It’s meaningless! You keep waiting for a hockey brawl to break out, but nothing like that ever happens.

Guard and inmate contestants in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

At first, the new guards try to act like “good” guards but soon realize this makes them seem like hypocrites. Instead, they ease up on restrictions, leading to a bit of a party atmosphere. Meanwhile, many of the inmates realize this is all kind of dumb (as will a great number of home viewers, I’m sure!) and start saying “pineapple.” Others are determined to make it to the end, to fulfill some sort of promise they’ve made to themselves. (Does Netflix cut them a bonus check if they last 14 days? None of that is ever discussed.)

Finally (to risk spoiling things), a decision emerges from the ranks. If the inmates all decide to leave as one, as a collective instead of individuals who have had enough, then they will have “taken power” and used it in the name of righteousness. Beaming with pride, our three overseers are delighted to conclude that, wowee, power doesn’t always corrupt! What a relief! The world’s systems can stay in place now. Or something.

If all this sounds preposterous, just know I’m leaving tons of extra nonsense out. I watched this series in awe of its stupidity. I am not one who automatically dismisses all competition shows. The Great British Baking Show is charming and RuPaul’s Drag Race is chock full of puns and creativity. But The New Stanford Prison Experiment is a round peg in a square hole—a ludicrous scenario desperate to rationalize its own existence.

Zimbardo’s experiment may have been unethical, but this is just humiliating, both to the audience and to the people who had to spend nearly two weeks in uncomfortable conditions before landing on a milquetoast and meaningless conclusion. If I were forced to watch all six episodes again, it would feel like a jail sentence.

This post appeared in the FP Weekend newsletter, a weekly showcase of book reviews, deep dives, and features. Sign up here.

Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman
